POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Thu, 12 Nov 2026 10:32:53 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 China’s diaspora crackdown reaches deep into Europe, report finds https://www.politico.eu/article/china-diaspora-crackdown-reaches-deep-into-europe-report-finds/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 12 Nov 2026 10:30:21 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9302487 THE HAGUE — Beijing is overseeing nearly 1,250 overseas policing outposts in more than 90 countries to crack down on dissidents, according to a report by a human rights advocacy organization.

The report described Europe as a hotspot with hundreds of Beijing’s policing offices across some two dozen European countries, which it said exposed China’s growing attempts to control its diaspora.

Researchers at the Spain-based organization, Safeguard Defenders, gathered open-source evidence from the Chinese Party-state to examine the extent to which the Chinese diaspora is monitored, surveilled and policed around the world.

These policing outposts “act as the Chinese Communist Party operatives for community surveillance and enforcement abroad,” according to the report.

The report lands at an awkward time for Europe’s trade officials. Ditte Juul Jørgensen, head of the EU’s trade department — which has been working to balance the trade relationship with Beijing — will meet with China’s Vice Minister of Commerce Ling Ji in Brussels on Thursday.

Europe is attempting to walk a fine line with its relations with Beijing. EU legislation proposed in January seeks to kick risky Chinese suppliers out of Europe’s most critical industries over cybersecurity concerns, while supply chain dependencies and political coercion remain ongoing challenges. The EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas has also raised concerns about what she said was China’s enabling of Russia’s war in Ukraine and credible reports of China training Russia’s military.

Overseas outposts

The report builds on initial revelations from Safeguard Defenders in 2022 that identified more than 100 facilities around the world, which the NGO described as overseas outposts of China’s security apparatus. Back then, that report said Beijing announced its “first batch” of “30 overseas police service stations in 25 cities in 21 countries.” 

Following the revelations, some governments denounced the overseas police stations as illegal, and some pursued criminal investigations, the NGO said in its latest report. In response, Beijing claimed the stations had been closed, it added.

“Far from closing, the evidence shows expansion: today more than 10 police forces from five Chinese provinces work through a global network of Chinese Communist Party operatives abroad,” the new report says.

The latest paper was presented at a conference hosted by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (IPAC), a gathering of 52 cross-party lawmakers from 30 countries that campaigns for a more coordinated response to the Chinese Communist Party. Policymakers raised numerous concerns at the event in The Hague earlier this month — about what they considered security threats of critical infrastructure, trade dependencies and potential risks from a future conflict between China and Taiwan that would disrupt shipping.

The Chinese foreign ministry and state media have previously called IPAC an “anti-China” group and accused it of spreading disinformation and interfering in China’s internal affairs, particularly over Taiwan.

China’s Ministry for Foreign Affairs and its European Union mission didn’t respond to requests for comment on the report. China has previously denied running overseas police stations and says it doesn’t interfere in other countries’ internal affairs and that it respects international law.

In 2023, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson rejected the term “police stations,” saying the “institutions helped overseas Chinese who could not return to China due to the pandemic, renew their driving licence and perform physical examination.” 

Tip of the iceberg

These 1,250 offices were “the tip of the iceberg,” according to the NGO, which said it was conservative in how it mapped and linked them to China’s policing system. To be counted, they had to be officially connected to China’s police or prosecutors and have open-source evidence of overseas activities, report author Laura Harth said. This meant broader influence or interference operations were excluded.

“All of them serve to control and instill fear in diaspora communities … all of them represent a standing national security risk,” she said.

Slovakian MEP Miriam Lexmann, who is part of the European Parliament’s trade committee and China delegation — lawmakers tasked with maintaining and managing legislative ties between the EU and China — said people needed to become more aware of the security threats posed by China.

“It means that our free countries are no longer free anymore for everyone because they are not able to guarantee freedom of speech, freedom of behavior to people who are in our country,” she told POLITICO in reference to the operations.

China’s surveillance through facial recognition and interference in communications was “the exact behavior of the former Soviet Stasi,” she said, but worse since the technology is now much more sophisticated.

The main concern expressed by lawmakers attending the IPAC conference was China’s relationship with Russia, and its help in propping up the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine. Their discussions included what this could mean for a future conflict and war on two fronts if Beijing were to try and take Taiwan militarily while NATO countries were attacked by Russia.

“The road to escalation in the Taiwan Strait can run right through what’s happening in Ukraine and in Kyiv,” said Dutch lawmaker Jan Paternotte, who co-chaired the IPAC conference.

]]> en Crisis engulfs Dutch government ahead of crucial tax vote https://www.politico.eu/article/dutch-coalition-government-hangs-thread-crucial-tax-vote-jetten-cda-pro-volt/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 12 Nov 2026 08:55:36 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9313860 The Netherlands’ minority coalition is under severe strain after two of its three members struck a deal with opposition parties to secure support for a contentious tax plan.

Ahead of a debate and vote Thursday, the centrist D66 party, led by Prime Minister Rob Jetten, and the center-right Christian Democratic Appeal (CDA) agreed with progressive opposition parties PRO and Volt to shift about €1 billion in tax from wealth to income. The deal reflects a key demand from PRO, the largest opposition party. The agreement has left the coalition’s third party, the center-right VVD, on the sidelines.

On Wednesday evening, VVD leader Dilan Yeşilgöz said she was surprised by the deal, which she called “bad for the Netherlands” and said “goes against the coalition agreement.” She threatened to reconsider cooperation with her coalition partners.

“This is not the way we should be working with each other,” she said. If D66 and CDA vote with PRO and Volt in Thursday’s parliamentary ballot, “we will also have to see how this cooperation can continue.”

D66 and CDA said late Wednesday that they would stand by the deal and would not renegotiate, adding to the pressure on the already-fragile coalition.

Jetten is expected to attend the debate and vote in the House of Representatives, and will miss Thursday’s European Political Community meeting in Dublin with other continental leaders.

The D66-VVD-CDA coalition is a minority government, holding 66 of 150 seats in the House of Representatives and 22 of 75 in the Senate. It is a rare arrangement in modern Dutch politics.

]]> en Climate action must work for ‘people on all incomes,’ Burnham tells COP31 https://www.politico.eu/article/climate-action-must-work-for-people-on-all-incomes-burnham-tells-cop31/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 12 Nov 2026 08:25:01 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9313812 ANTALYA, Turkey — World leaders and industry must make electric cars and heat pumps affordable if they are to ensure “people on all incomes” can “make the green transition,” U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the COP31 climate summit.

During a flying visit to this year’s U.N. conference in Turkey, Burnham — who has made affordability his core domestic political focus — reaffirmed the U.K.’s commitment to the goal of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.

But he warned that the world had “not moved as quick as I had hoped in the past five years” to show citizens that climate action and electrification have cost-of-living upsides.

“The last of these meetings I attended was COP26 as the mayor of Greater Manchester,” Burnham said, referring to the 2021 summit hosted by the U.K. He warned at the time that the climate movement must not lose sight of the “struggles of ordinary families.”

“The world feels very different now, and we need to adapt,” Burnham said. “Electrification in transport, heat and industry is how we make clean power, cheap power.”

While voicing support for COP31 hosts Turkey and Australia’s electrification push, Burnham stopped short of backing the specific target of 35% of global energy use shifting to electricity by 2035.

But he emphasized the benefits the switch could bring, while urging industry to help ensure it helped all consumers.

“If you drive a new electric car today in the U.K., it costs less than a petrol equivalent. Get on the right tariff and a heat pump can be cheaper to run than a gas boiler. These technologies are becoming cheaper, but they are not available to everybody on all incomes,” he said.

“As a government, we are doing our bit by investing in innovation and subsidizing upfront costs for the public. But we need industry to play their part too, and help people on all incomes to make the green transition.”

The focus on EVs and heat pumps comes despite Burnham’s government cutting the subsidy pot for heat pumps at last month’s budget. Ministers are also weighing proposals to water down industry EV quotas.

Nonetheless, Burnham reiterated the U.K.’s over-arching strategy to cut dependence on fossil fuels.  

“The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is upon us all now, devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere. Meanwhile, two wars across two continents have sent fuel prices and gas bills soaring for families and businesses across the world,” he said. “The common thread running through all of this: our dependence on fossil fuels.”

He announced the U.K. would use its G20 presidency next year to “put climate resilience back on the agenda, with debt, development, and insurance as key issues.”

Burnham’s government has also created a new role of special representative for climate security, appointing former head of the Joint Intelligence Committee Chair Madeline Alessandri to the post.

]]> en Estonia wants Costa and Kallas to speak for Europe in Ukraine peace talks  https://www.politico.eu/article/estonia-antonio-costa-kaja-kallas-europe-ukraine-peace-talks/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 12 Nov 2026 08:23:18 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9312063 Estonia called for European Council President António Costa and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas to represent Europe in Russia-Ukraine negotiations, as leaders grapple with who should have a seat at the negotiating table.

“Europe has already chosen its representatives: Council President António Costa and [High Representative] Kaja Kallas. Both are clearly accountable to EU countries,” Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told POLITICO.

The matter is set to come up at an informal European Council summit in Dublin on Friday, at the behest of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who said in a letter to Costa that Europe’s approach has been “all over the place” and risked prolonging the war. Costa subsequently agreed to prioritize the topic at the talks in Ireland. 

Michal said Costa and Kallas’ “mandate comes directly from the Council,” meaning that “there is no need for an ad hoc plan to be agreed between member states first.”

The question of who should speak for Europe has taken on greater urgency as U.S.-led efforts to broker an end to the war gather pace. This week’s three-way talks in Abu Dhabi involved representatives from Russia, the U.S. and Ukraine — with the EU represented by senior civil servants in a separate, wider meeting.

The leaders of Finland and Norway held a 90-minute phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin last month, in a rare contact between Europe and the Kremlin.

But in a sign of the divisions among leaders about who should lead Europe’s negotiating efforts, the three-way conversation drew sharp criticism from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who said she was “skeptical” of the initiative. “I think we should keep Europe united rather than going it alone,” she said. 

Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump and one of the main American negotiators with Russia and Ukraine, said this week that “if Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations.” 

Too bad

The summit in Dublin is not expected to produce a formal decision to select an envoy, according to a senior EU official granted anonymity to discuss the plan for the proceedings, but rather an “understanding” among leaders about who should relay Europe’s position to the Kremlin, with the actual choice to be made later. 

According to EU law, the bloc is represented on the world stage by the European Council president — Costa, currently. “The interests of the European Union must be represented by its institutions, in accordance with the Treaties,” he wrote in response to Meloni’s letter, appearing to hint that he was up for the job.

Costa’s head of Cabinet Pedro Lourtie contacted officials in Moscow twice in June to establish a channel of communication, infuriating some leaders, POLITICO reported at the time.

Kallas also has foreign policy competence as the bloc’s High Representative. But her critics have long argued the former Estonian prime minister is too hawkish on Russia and would not be able to negotiate in good faith with Moscow. 

“There is no need to appoint anyone new. If Russians don’t like it, too bad,” Michal said. “We should be represented by those we trust and who are accountable to the EU, not by those who Putin likes.”

Not everyone is on board with the EU institutions taking a leading role in the negotiations. Marine Le Pen, France’s poll-leading far-right presidential candidate, wants to drastically reduce Brussels’ diplomatic role. 

Fabrice Leggeri, an MEP from Le Pen’s RN party, insisted Costa and Kallas could not speak for France. 

“There is no diplomatic competence for the European Union,” he told POLITICO. “We should keep this at the level of our nations … I can hardly imagine that we would expect that the EU, that Costa or Kallas, would speak on behalf of France.“

]]> en Poland turns to home-grown giant for its defense buildup https://www.politico.eu/article/poland-home-grown-giant-defense-buildup/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 12 Nov 2026 03:50:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9207281 WARSAW — Poland wants domestic companies to supply more of its rapidly expanding military, but state-owned PGZ’s fragmented structure and political exposure raise questions about whether Warsaw can turn the spending surge into a stronger industry.

The Polish Armaments Group, the country’s largest defense company, has won billions of złoty in new orders, placing it at the center of the military buildup.

The conglomerate was cobbled together in 2013 from about 50 fiercely independent smaller companies with their own management teams and often their own political backers. CEO Adam Leszkiewicz has been in the post since May 2025 — making him the holding company’s 12th CEO since its founding.

“PGZ is different from other European companies,” Leszkiewicz said, adding that PGZ makes more than 700 products. “I could say we make almost everything. But what can be a strength can also be a weakness.”

Marek Świerczyński, a defense analyst with the Warsaw-based Polityka Insight Center for Policy Analysis, said: “He essentially has to use diplomacy to try to manage the other companies.”

Legacy defense industry

For decades after the end of communism, Poland spent little on defense and the military largely made do with antiquated Soviet-era equipment. Russia’s illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 and its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 changed that, and Polish defense spending surged.

“We have strong historical and current experience with armored vehicles and maintenance, repair and overhaul services,” said Leszkiewicz. “We also make wheeled vehicles such as the Jelcz, and our work on sensors and radar is developing well. We have long been strong in rifles and pistols.”

Aleksandra Kozioł, a defense analyst with the Warsaw-based Polish Institute of International Affairs, pointed out other notable Polish defense companies, such as the private WB Group, which specializes in communications networks, unmanned aerial vehicles, loitering munitions and fire control solutions.

“We want to improve in new technologies, especially unmanned vehicles as well as software and IT solutions,” Leszkiewicz said.

PGZ is also building ties with other European defense firms. It is building three new artillery shell factories in conjunction with the U.K.’s BAE Systems. PGZ’s Narew air defense system includes a tie-up with MBDA to supply missiles and launchers.

“Either we take advantage of this opportunity, or we let this period of rapid industrial development in defense pass. We have ambitions and want to fulfill them,” Leszkiewicz said.

Keeping the cash at home

This year, Poland aims to spend 200 billion złoty (€45.7 billion) — or 4.8% of GDP — on defense, the highest level in NATO. It is also the largest recipient of the EU’s €150 billion SAFE loans-for-arms program, taking in almost €44 billion.

The government is trying to ensure that the country’s defense industry gets a growing share of the new spending.

In May, Poland’s Armaments Agency signed almost 120 billion złoty in contracts with Polish arms companies financed by SAFE. A large share went to PGZ and its subsidiaries, mainly Huta Stalowa Wola, for equipment including 146 Borsuk infantry fighting vehicles, 96 Krab howitzers, 64 Rak mortars, K9PL support vehicles and 1,000 vehicles for the Homar-K rocket-launcher system.

Most of the deals with PGZ were no-bid contracts, according to a report by the Warsaw Enterprise Institute think tank.

“The development of the Polish defense industry is necessary, but it should not automatically mean preferential treatment for companies directly controlled by the government,” the report said.

Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz last month underlined that the government aims to develop the country’s military-industrial complex, saying: “We are building a strong army, strengthening security, and investing in Poland’s future.”

But favoring domestic companies risks clashing with the government’s drive to rearm as quickly as possible; Warsaw wants to buy tanks, jets and missiles to deter Russia, although that goal does pose problems for its domestic arms industry.

About 60 percent of Poland’s defense spending goes on imports, “and that won’t change quickly,” said Świerczyński. Most arms imports come from South Korea and the United States, including systems like K2 Black Panther tanks and F-35A fighter jets.

“In 2022, we were looking for ready-made solutions and products because we felt threatened,” said Leszkiewicz. “Today, we are trying to take every opportunity to Polonize production. We are now hardly buying ready-made products, except where we really lack a particular capability.” One of PGZ’s subsidiaries will be building K2 tanks starting in 2028. 

“I do see an effort to increase Polish intellectual property,” said Kozioł, the defense analyst, adding that it’s still unclear if the government’s effort to shift contracts to Polish firms will lessen the reliance on foreign technology.

In 2025, PGZ reported 18.4 billion złoty in revenues, a 23% increase on the previous year, and 2.8 billion złoty in profit, a 66% increase. The company ranked 51st in the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s 2025 list of the world’s top 100 defense companies.  

“We aim to reach the top 10 in Europe and the top 30 globally,” said Leszkiewicz.

“If we look at PGZ’s development and results, it appears that, despite political issues, the company is trying to fulfill the task of arming the Polish military,” said Kozioł.

Political risk

Polish state-controlled companies are notorious for high levels of political interference. Although Kozioł underlined that there is a cross-party consensus in favor of continued high defense spending, PGZ does face political risks.

Mateusz Morawiecki, prime minister from 2017 to 2023 under the previous Law and Justice Party government, this summer called for PGZ to potentially be dissolved, accusing it of “weak” management.

Kosiniak-Kamysz fired back, calling the idea “harmful and anti-state.”

The danger is likely to grow. Poland holds a parliamentary election next year and opinion polls suggest that Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s coalition could be unseated by a grouping of right-wing parties.

That means Leszkiewicz’s position — he was a junior member of Tusk’s previous government from 2007 to 2011 and took over PGZ after running state-controlled fertilizer giant Grupa Azoty — could be under threat.

“A CEO would have to be in the job for a decade, but in Polish realities there is no chance of that,” said Świerczyński.

]]> en The Kremlin can hide the death toll. It can’t hide the graves. https://www.politico.eu/article/kremlin-hide-numbers-cant-hide-graves-russia-ukraine-war/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 12 Nov 2026 03:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9241242 In September, a Russian court condemned a middle-aged man in Yaroslavl to 14 years in a penal colony — a sentence usually reserved for the country’s most twisted killers. His crime? Taking photographs of gravestones of Russian soldiers who died in Ukraine.

With the Kremlin coy about battlefield casualty figures, independent journalists and activists have used photography to document the war’s true death toll, revealing losses far greater than Moscow has publicly acknowledged.

“The multiplying number of graves — that must be a sight that’s bothering the authorities very much because it reminds them of the failure of Putin’s war,” Jan C. Behrends of the German-based Leibniz Centre for Contemporary History said. “So many people have died.”

In recent months, Russian authorities have issued warnings that taking photographs of military graves could result in life imprisonment, while the Federal Security Service has patrolled the country’s cemeteries in search of offenders. Since the summer, several dozen people across Russia have been arrested. The official charge in these closed trials is treason — specifically, cooperation with Ukrainian intelligence services.

Russia’s losses since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine are staggering. Russia 200, a casualty-tracking database created by independent outlet Mediazona and the BBC’s Russian service, lists the names of nearly 283,000 dead soldiers, including details about the circumstances of their deaths. But Mediazona, which draws on open-source information like social media posts and reports in local media, does not have the resources and access to document every battlefield fatality.

Other organizations estimate the death toll to be significantly higher. The U.K. Foreign Office and Dutch intelligence services estimate Russia’s losses to stand at more than half a million, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced in July that 700,000 Russian soldiers had died fighting in Ukraine.

Even the most modest estimates of Russian losses in Ukraine far surpass Soviet casualties in Afghanistan, a conflict that lasted nearly a decade from its launch in 1979. Then, as now, the Kremlin strove to hide the true costs of war.

Relatives of those who died in Afghanistan were forbidden from engraving the place of their loved ones’ deaths on their gravestones. “You could not mark the grave in any way that indicated that the person had died in the war,” Jeff Jones, a professor of history at the University of North Carolina, said. “Some [relatives] were actually forced to hold funerals at night so that it wouldn’t draw attention,” he added.

Later, relatives were permitted to engrave the words, “died heroically while fulfilling an international duty,” but “died in Afghanistan” was never allowed.

At the beginning of the war in Ukraine, the Kremlin wasn’t quite so guarded. In September 2022, six months after the start of Moscow’s full-scale invasion, Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu said 5,937 Russian soldiers had died in the conflict.

Since then, there have been few official pronouncements about Russian casualties. As its “special military operation” turned into a protracted conflict, Moscow has ramped up efforts to conceal the numbers, shutting down new avenues of investigation for anyone trying to document casualty figures.

In April 2024, a Kremlin spokesperson reminded journalists that information on casualties is a “state secret” and reporting on losses remains the “exclusive prerogative of the Ministry of Defense.”

Later that year, Rosstat, Russia’s official statistical body, barred access to its data on the country’s excess death rate, which had been accessible since the 1990s as part of liberalization efforts under perestroika and glasnost.

The Rosstat data was an invaluable source for verifying information on casualties — and for refuting government claims, says Dmitry Treshchanin, Mediazona editor and co-author of Russia 200.

“We can count everyone name by name, but someone from government would always say ‘it’s fake,'” Treshchanin said. “But when you have official data confirming our calculations, nothing can be done with it.”

Moscow has also stifled information on court cases concerning dead soldiers. In early 2025, Russian journalists noticed an unprecedented uptick in the number of court cases emerging about soldiers being declared missing in action or dead. Military units normally ask courts to declare soldiers dead when they do not return from a battlefield for months.

“It was growing exponentially — it was big news,” Treshchanin said. “You start with 40,000 cases, then four months later you have 70,000, and two months after that, 90,000. I mean, just how many of these people could there possibly be?” 

Russia 200 recorded almost 90,000 such cases in 2025 — a more than tenfold increase compared to earlier years of the invasion.  “And at some point, they just classified it,” Treshchanin said, referring to the government’s decision to restrict access to these court proceedings at the end of 2025.

As for graveyard photography, Treshchanin and his colleagues are now cautious about using such methods.

“Photos of graves and videos of the funerals were an important source of information for us at the very beginning of the Russian invasion, when not much other info was available,” he explained. But once the Kremlin got wise to the technique, it became too dangerous. “Our volunteers were attacked at the cemeteries,” he explained.

The reason the Kremlin guards information about its losses so jealously is to more easily hire soldiers for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Ian Matveev, a Russian military analyst and an associate of the late Russian dissident Alexei Navalny, said.

“This is a way to deceive potential recruits. If people could easily find out what percentage of contract soldiers survive at the front — or how long a new recruit is likely to last — it would be extremely difficult to enlist even 30,000 troops per month,” Matveev said. By concealing losses, Moscow may also try to impress an “external audience — specifically, at Donald Trump — to convince him that Putin’s army is on the verge of winning the war,” he added.

With each new restriction from the Kremlin, journalists are forced to adjust their methods. “Russia is big,” said Treshchanin. “If something gets stifled in one place, it means that, conversely, something else ends up growing elsewhere.”

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Thu, 12 Nov 2026 09:39:20 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Listen: Why can’t Europe offer Ukraine an alternative to Starlink?  https://euobserver.com/248483/listen-why-cant-europe-offer-ukraine-an-alternative-to-starlink/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 08:42:34 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248483 Ukraine’s war effort depends heavily on two American tools: Starlink and Starshield. Both belong to Elon Musk’s SpaceX, and both can be switched off. Europe says it wants to reduce that dependence.]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below:

Ukraine’s war effort depends heavily on two American tools: Starlink and Starshield. Both belong to Elon Musk’s SpaceX, and both can be switched off. Europe says it wants to reduce that dependence.

Is it possible, and why is Europe so far behind? Starlink is SpaceX’s satellite internet service. It’s sold to the general public, to companies and to armies. It relies on a constellation of around 10,000 satellites in low orbit, which makes it possible to get a connection almost anywhere on Earth.

Starshield is the version designed for governments and militaries. It uses the same technology, but with dedicated satellites and dedicated encryption. In other words, it’s more secure.

Read more

Russia faces a strategic crisis and record losses, but thanks to Trump it sees things positively (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,713)

The problem is that its use completely depends on the goodwill of Elon Musk. But also on the US government. Starshield is a government system, and it’s Washington that actually makes it available to Ukraine.

This has already led to some awkward situations. A few weeks ago, Ukraine noticed that the speed of its drones had been throttled overnight. The explanation was clear: it was an American move. The issue has since been resolved, but it illustrates a real unease.

So how did Ukraine end up in this position? At the start of the war, the country’s cable-based internet infrastructure was damaged. On the battlefield, the army now uses SpaceX terminals to receive internet signal, because they’re small and very practical.

And that is exactly what Europeans don’t offer. Most European satellites are in high orbit. They cover very large areas, but they have two drawbacks in wartime. Because they are further away, the delay in transmission is longer. Second, the equipment needed to receive the signal is much bulkier, so it is not suited to the front line.

Elon Musk made a very strategic choice: putting tens of thousands of satellites in low orbit.  It’s much cheaper, and much easier to operate. Now could Europeans compete on this market?

The closest European equivalent, on a smaller scale, is the OneWeb constellation, run by the French company Eutelsat. Eutelsat was originally a European intergovernmental organisation. But it was dismantled and its activity has been taken over by a company.

The French state is still its largest shareholder, with around a third of the shares. The United Kingdom and an Indian group also hold stakes.

Through OneWeb, Eutelsat has around 680 satellites, in both low and high orbit. The company says it could replace Starlink in the medium term, meaning sometime in the 2030s.

It plans to reinforce its fleet with several hundred new satellites. But most of them will actually replace older ones. So it’s not a big increase, compared with Starlink.

Read more

Russia’s fake war maps at Abu Dhabi peace talks aren’t fooling anyone (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,721)

There is also another project designed to secure European connections. It’s called IRIS². This one is a European project, carried out by several companies, including Eutelsat. The EU is its main customer. Unlike OneWeb, it’s not a commercial venture. But both share the same goal: reducing dependence on Starlink.

The ambition is a constellation of at least 348 satellites by 2030, with deployment starting in 2029. So again, fewer than a thousand. That’s still far from Starlink.

But here, it’s worth saying that satellites in low orbit are much cheaper to put in place, which also explains the sheer volume SpaceX has been able to launch in recent years.

With far fewer satellites, but in higher orbit, Europeans can also cover the whole planet. It’s just that the system isn’t as flexible.

Finally, is money part of the explanation? Yes, of course. The United States spends around six times more on its space programmes, civil and military, than Europeans do.

There’s also another factor that helps SpaceX deploy thousands of satellites at low cost: it has its own launcher, the Falcon 9.

Eutelsat, on the other hand, has to buy launches from third parties. So it’s much more expensive, and it doesn’t control the pace at which it can put satellites into orbit.

Before wrapping up, a quick word about China, another big actor. It’s quite new in the space industry, and it’s not really spending huge amounts of money for the moment. But it’s worth keeping an eye on Beijing on this front too.

South of the grey, industrial northern cities, from the rolling hills of Tuscany down to the rocky heel of the Ionian sea, one is never too far from the scent trailing behind the world’s most sought after harvests: the grape, and the olive. 

I was visiting my family in the fields of Rome, where this year’s crop alleviated concern brought on by last year’s meagre yield. My uncle’s generous green bounty was turned to liquid gold, one that tastes of legacy and belonging.

On the eastern seaboard of the Mediterranean, it has also come to smell like blood.

The ancient tradition, and the historic land that binds it to its sturdy tree roots, has been turned into the battleground of Israeli colonisation of the occupied West Bank. Exacerbated since 2023, the olive harvest has become the season synonymous with the most attacks by Israeli defence forces-backed illegal settlers hoping to intimidate Palestinian families out of their homes. 

Read more

From West Bank to EU supermarkets: How much longer will Israeli settler imports go on?

It’s the time where residents, forced indoors in fear of the swelling conflict increasingly taking place beyond just Gaza, dare to set foot out to reap the fruits of the land that provides a living for some 100,000 families across the Palestinian territories.

Beyond the major source of income many depend upon, depriving Palestine of its olive harvest denies some 5.6 million people with the social fabric that makes up the part of their national identity. 

According to UN data, the 2025 olive harvest brought 178 settler attacks to the occupied West Bank, in 88 Palestinian towns and villages. Over 6,000 trees and saplings were vandalised.

]]> War of propaganda: Russia calls Ukraine a ‘burden’ and uses Moldova as a ‘testing ground’ to sabotage EU enlargement https://euobserver.com/247967/war-of-propaganda-russia-calls-ukraine-a-burden-and-uses-moldova-as-a-testing-ground-to-sabotage-eu-enlargement/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:32:04 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247967 From fake celebrity sex scandals to ominous warnings about land seizures and soaring bills, Kremlin-linked campaigns are working to turn ordinary voters against EU accession long before any referendum is held.]]> As the saying goes, the first casualty of war is the truth. But in the case of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it seems the truth had been under attack for a while. 

As recently as this summer, claims that Russia had actually made significant battlefield gains were debunked after analysis found that interpretation was based on misuse of a report which actually found Ukraine had made the greater advances.

It chimes with the continuing battle for control of the narrative over Ukraine, not least when it comes to the prospect of that country, and possibly its neighbour, Moldova, ultimately joining the EU.

Media organisations in those countries have become acutely aware of what they say is Russian disinformation about EU enlargement, often circulated via the Telegram app and other online platforms such as Facebook.

They have heard various narratives against EU membership, such as a purported loss of state sovereignty, of the EU wishing to prolong a ‘proxy war’ with Russia through Ukraine, and even of Ukraine being divided up between EU member states.

As Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine approaches its sixth year, the likelihood of it joining the EU is still being actively debated. Neighbouring Moldova is also driving towards EU membership, even though it is aware that Russia is actively opposed. 

It means both countries, and others in the region where people have expressed a desire to join the EU, such as Georgia, find themselves the subject of online campaigns which, critics say, are aimed at undermining those efforts.

Read more

Moldova seen as ‘best performer’ on EU-accession reforms, despite onslaught of Russian sabotage

Disinformation is not new

It is also hard to argue that this is a new phenomenon. Over 10 years ago, the EU set up a task force in order to challenge “Russia’s ongoing disinformation campaigns”. 

A number of months after the war began in 2022, the OECD think-tank in Paris published a policy paper on ‘Disinformation and Russia’s War of Aggression against Ukraine’, in which it said: “The Russian disinformation narratives are often false, or obscure facts with half-truths and ‘whataboutisms’.” 

And just last year the delegation of the European Union to Ukraine looked at information manipulation and disinformation that summer targeting Ukraine-EU relations.

It was a topic of discussion when the deputy prime minister for European integration of Moldova, Cristina Gherasimov, visited Ireland earlier this year. 

Speaking to The Journal in Dublin last February, Gherasimov said that disinformation “continues constantly”.

Read more

How EU hopes to ‘shield’ elections against Moscow’s propaganda

“This is one of the most powerful tools of Moscow: disinformation, not necessarily about our own country or process in our own country, but a narrative that targets the EU as such. It targets the EU credibility for candidate countries or aspiring countries, for EU membership.

“Some of the narratives are usually around the future of candidate countries in the EU, saying that we are not ready,” she said.

This argument, she added, also centred on the idea of the EU as weak and unable to stand up for its own citizens.

Another line is that new entrant countries would be seen as a ‘poor relation’ and would not be as competitive when it comes to agriculture and other areas once they joined the EU.

“What we’ve learned from our own elections is that disinformation does not stop after the elections, it continues constantly, and it adapts very quickly in terms of the narratives that it promotes, depending on the vulnerabilities that exist in each society that is targeted,” she added.

“One very usual narrative targeting the EU is that all the land will be expropriated once Moldova joins the European Union, and that is meant to draw equal lines with how it used to be during the Soviet Union period for us, and that is meant to inflict fear that the EU is not there to support and protect its citizens, but it’s there to actually prey on them,” said Gherasimov.

Ukrainian accession efforts labelled ‘futile’?

Moldova knows about disinformation: a report in the New York Times last September said the Stimson Center – a research organisation in Washington – called the country “a testing ground for hybrid warfare operations” that “are likely to shape similar efforts” across Europe. 

The same New York Times article referred to how, ahead of Moldova’s parliamentary election, social media platforms were flooded with fabricated posts, videos and websites, sometimes created using AI. 

As outlined in this Euronews report, one post even impersonated the celebrity magazine OK! with a false story declaring “Moldovan president in celebrity sperm scandal!”. The concocted story, which incorrectly claimed that president Maia Sandu was buying sperm from gay celebrity donors to have a child, falsely used the name of a real reporter. 

This demonstrates how disinformation frequently attempts to erode political reputations and steer voters towards particular political agendas. 

Read more

EU accession of Moldova and Ukraine is alternative to Nato, as Russia draws new Iron Curtain in Europe

As with other forms of political disinformation, this takes many forms when it comes to EU accession, according to Vladyslav Lesyk, a journalist at Ukrainian media outlet Rubryka.

“One of the primary Russian narratives regarding Ukraine’s EU accession is the claim that Ukraine’s efforts to join the Union are futile,” he said. 

“For instance, Russian sources have spread fakes asserting that granting candidate status is a merely formal decision that offers no actual benefits. The functions of this narrative are to demoralise Ukrainian society and create the impression that the reforms required for EU membership are pointless,” he added.

“Another Russian narrative suggests that joining the EU would mean Ukraine losing its sovereignty. This builds upon a broader Russian narrative, maintained since the start of the Russo-Ukrainian war in 2014, which portrays Ukraine as a state with an illegitimate government controlled by the West, specifically the EU and the US,” said Lesyk.

Read more

Wave of Russian sabotage attacks exposes counter-intelligence gaps on Nato’s eastern flank

Disinformation is not new: EUvsDisinfo documents numerous past examples, including the infamous false story from 2014 of a boy allegedly being crucified by Ukrainian nationals in Slovyansk. This was cited to be part of a Kremlin-orchestrated campaign targeted at inciting hatred against Ukrainians.

Ukraine has long articulated a desire to join the EU and the process is well underway. Since June 2022, Ukraine has official EU candidate status, with accession negotiations having formally started. Last September Ukraine successfully completed its screening process.

Billions of euros in financial assistance have already been provided, while the EU has repeatedly affirmed its support for Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.

The ‘burden’ narrative

On the flip side, Lesyk said narratives spread in European countries lean into the idea of Ukraine becoming a “burden” on EU member states. 

“In this context, Ukraine is presented as a poor and corrupt state whose accession would supposedly drain the European budget. A specific sub-narrative focuses on the negative impact of Ukrainian grain on European farming. Russians have been spreading the narrative of ‘harmful’ Ukrainian grain for several years to sow discord,” he said.

Yet as this analysis from the European Policy Centre points out, Ukraine joining the EU would have very obvious benefits – including opening up the country’s energy potential to the EU, boosting EU food security, and providing ready trade in critical minerals.

Lesyk said Telegram is the primary hub for disseminating these Russian narratives in Ukraine, as it allows for the use of anonymous channels and is one of the most popular sources of information in the country. 

Regarding Moldova, media and fact-checking organisations have tracked a number of lines of attack regarding proposed EU membership, ranging from farms there closing due to Moldovan agricultural products not being in demand, to higher utility bills, and same-sex marriage. 

These were analysed in depth by the website NewsMaker.md. Romanian fact-checking website Veridica has tracked numerous disinformation campaigns, including that Moldova could become a destination for migrants, could lose its statehood, or even be annexed by Romania.

Read more

[Interview] ‘Whenever we take pro-European political decisions, Russia cut or reduced gas supplies’. Moldova energy minister Dorin Junghietu on why Chișinău is betting on diversification

Homegrown issues

In Georgia, another country seemingly at a crossroads when it comes to possible EU membership, websites such as OC Media have tracked what they believe are coordinated Russian information operations in recent years.

Salome Khvedelidze of OC Media said some of this runs on Facebook and other platforms. The International Society for Fair Elections and Democracy detailed material it described as “the dissemination of anti-Western, particularly anti-EU narratives”.

Common themes include the EU being a threat to Georgian values, such as EU support for LGBTQ+ rights, the potential for EU interference in Georgian domestic affairs, and the idea of the EU and the US more broadly wanting to spark conflict.

Read more

Zelensky stalls on his EU promises to protect gay rights, even as Ukraine rushes through minority-languages law

Since Russia’s war against Ukraine in 2022, Georgia has turned increasingly authoritarian, suspending EU accession talks and deepening its ties with Moscow.

Recently, the ruling Georgian Dream party sought to ban the five main opposition parties – a move which is currently being fought in court. The European Parliament warned that this puts the country’s path towards EU membership at risk.

According to Khvedelidze: “What makes Georgia different from Ukraine and Moldova, however, is where the main source of anti-EU propaganda actually comes from.”

“In Ukraine and Moldova, disinformation about EU membership is driven by Russian proxies, Russia-backed/funded media, and certain political figures, while the governments themselves are pro-European,” she said.

Arguably, it gives the impression of a message that is always changing but always the same. According to Cristina Gherasimov: “It adapts very quickly in terms of the narratives that it promotes, depending on the vulnerabilities that exist in each society that is targeted,” she added.

It is not always straightforward to verify which narratives come directly from Russia and which originate elsewhere, but there is little doubt about Russia’s attitude towards the EU, and its history of spreading disinformation abroad.

]]> [Interview] ‘I cannot be optimistic,’ says climatologist Jean Jouzel https://euobserver.com/246223/interview-i-cannot-be-optimistic-says-climatologist-jean-jouzel/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:31:15 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246223 Jean Jouzel, a renowned French climatologist, is not optimistic about the changing climate and the level of mitigation efforts. But he says people should should not give up on the fight against global warming.]]> First published in Respekt.

Jean Jouzel, a renowned French climatologist, is not optimistic about the changing climate and the level of mitigation efforts. But the scientist says people should should not give up on the fight against global warming. He explains the green deal, carbon markets, temperature rises and where the fight for a better environment stands now.

You previously said you hope that once Covid-19 passes, society would become more friendly to the environment.

Jean Jouzel: Unfortunately, this is not happening. Globally, carbon dioxide emissions continue to rise. They should stabilise over time, but that has not happened. Changes are taking place, but they are insufficient. Europe used to champion the ambitious Green Deal, but that ambition at a European level has faded.

So your optimism has gone?

When the Paris Climate Agreement was made in 2015, I was optimistic. But real progress is not being made. It is not that nothing at all has been done, but compared with the gravity of the problem, progress has been very slow. Many politicians focus only on how to adapt to climate change, which is important, but not enough.

Unless we have a good strategy and do something big by around 2040, it will be difficult to achieve carbon neutrality by the end of the century, essential to stabilising the climate.

Read more

EU states back one-year methane delay, but leave door open for more

What will this mean?

The people who are young today will live on a continuously warming planet. It is difficult to grasp that what we do over the next 15 years will have effects after such a long delay in the second half of this century.

Politicians say we have time; they argue that young people are so proficient in working with artificial intelligence that they will somehow solve the problem. But sea level rise cannot be stopped. By doing nothing, we are taking an enormous risk.

We live in a highly unstable, warring world. Does it make sense to pursue climate change mitigation now?

At an international level, I genuinely do not see solidarity between states. Clearly, the world is turning away from climate policies. And without mutual solidarity, we cannot stop global warming. So I cannot be optimistic.

Read more

Climate inaction could cost Europe €5.6 trillion by 2050, study finds

Even those who recognise the gravity of the problem say: let us not push the climate agenda now, because we are only playing into the hands of extremist political forces such as the Alternative for Germany (AfD) or the National Rally in France. Let us not talk about the climate, because we are endangering the future of democracy itself. What do you think?

We must stress the benefits of climate change mitigation, like human health through cleaner air, and economic growth.

Over the next decade, the economy should be built around a transition to a different way of operating: economic systems based on carbon and fossil fuels will shift towards systems based on achieving carbon neutrality.

Take the electric car: it is an interesting technology. There is no reason to continue relying on transport based on the internal combustion engine. China is doing a great deal in this respect and is moving in the right direction. Europe is not.

We should have been the ones setting the pace. Economic growth can be built on the shift to electric cars. Or take the retrofitting and thermal insulation of buildings, which will have positive effects both on the economy and on human health. During the summer, 8,000 died in France because of the heat, and 17,000 in Germany. When heat waves are so severe, it is very difficult to live in cities. The issue of climate change cannot be separated from everyday life. It is not only about the environment, but also about the economy.

But how can people be persuaded? There is an enormous amount of disinformation surrounding the climate.

The spread of misinformation is made easier by social media, which are so popular among young people. Climate change scepticism also arises from this. It is difficult to fight. A false message is easy to spread, but defending against it and putting forward counterarguments is difficult. At a certain point, I gave up on the idea that we could convince 100 percent of the population. It is enough to win over a majority — and that should not be impossible.

Read more

What is ‘coordinated inauthentic behaviour’ – and how is it distorting Europe’s online democracy?

People can see that something is happening to the climate. We must continue presenting our arguments to them, explaining how greenhouse-gas emissions are affected by everyday activities. If we do nothing, we will face very serious consequences in the second half of the century. It will be difficult, because climate sceptics have one huge advantage: they claim that we can continue our way of life and not worry about the climate – a very appealing idea. But if you believe there is a problem, it makes you concerned.

So how should we deal with this?

As I said, we should stress that the transition to a more sustainable way of life will bring us many benefits. Energy is at the heart of this transition. Transport and the thermal insulation of buildings are also important, but energy is where we need to start.

In your native France, do emissions taxes under the ETS2 system provoke concerns over fuel prices?

The increase in fuel prices was enormous in France, but one public response has been increased purchases of electric cars. In September, electric vehicles accounted for 40 percent of new sales. At the beginning of the year, it was only 28 percent. That is a major change. People are not buying electric cars because of the climate, but because of high petrol and diesel prices. I am afraid, however, that once prices fall, people will start returning to internal combustion engines. Prices influence their behaviour more than concern for the climate.

Read more

Compromise over chaos? How MEPs gutted Europe’s new carbon price before it even began

But the electricity for cars must be generated without emissions. Which technology is most promising? Renewables? Nuclear power?

In France, we generate most of our electricity from nuclear power, around 70 percent, but renewables are developing rapidly. If we want to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050, we must develop both: build new nuclear power plants while expanding renewables as quickly as possible.

Once you have a nuclear power plant that has been built, the electricity it produces is very cheap. But if you are only planning to build one, it is very expensive. Isn’t solar and wind power better?

High costs are indeed the biggest obstacle to the expansion of nuclear energy. By contrast, the costs of renewables are continually falling. On the other hand, they require strengthening the electricity grid in order to balance out the fluctuations in their electricity generation. That also costs money. This is why I believe we need a mix of both technologies.

Although the climate measures adopted have slowed global warming, the world is still heading towards warming of almost three degrees Celsius by 2100. What will that world look like?

Could you start by explaining what dark patterns are?

Christoph Busch: Dark patterns is a catchy term that refers to various types of manipulative design features – how user-interface design is used to steer consumers in various directions.

As for the EU Kids Act, it focuses on the protection of minors. But addictive design features also affect adults, including gamification in online shopping. I think there is still a need for targeted amendments to the existing regulatory framework: not just another layer on top, but targeted, focused gap-filling.

    ]]>         Consumers pay the price for online manipulation, and the EU Digital Fairness Act can put a stop to it https://euobserver.com/247929/consumers-pay-the-price-for-online-manipulation-and-the-eu-digital-fairness-act-can-put-a-stop-to-it/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 12:35:02 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247929 The EU's Digital Fairness Act (DFA) is one of the few initiatives of this legislative term through which Europe can improve people's lives by strengthening their consumer rights and helping them save money, write the Socialists & Democrats.]]> Think about the last thing you did before going to sleep, and the first thing you did when you woke up. Look around you on the bus or the metro. We are hooked on our devices and the online services behind them.

    That is not a personal failing. It is by design, part of a business model.

    Digital products that we use daily – whether apps, social media platforms or online marketplaces – make their profits by exploiting our attention, our mental health and our vulnerabilities.

    Feeds that never end, subscriptions that are near impossible to cancel, and fake countdowns that push us to click and buy on impulse are no accident. They are deliberate design features with a direct impact on our wellbeing and our wallets.

    Today, the European Commission is presenting the Digital Fairness Act (DFA) as a proposal to fight these and other unfair online practices.

    It is one of the few initiatives of this legislative term through which Europe can improve people’s lives by strengthening their consumer rights and helping them save money.

    Unfair commercial practices are estimated to cost European consumers close to €8bn a year. Whether or not the DFA will become a game changer in the fight against addictive and manipulative design will depend on the ambition the EU shows.

    Read more

    Digital Fairness Act: EU cracks down on influencer ads and manipulative app design

    Despite the clear need for digital fairness, new rules will face opposition from some quarters, notably US Big Tech.

    It runs against their push to deregulate under the guise of “simplification”, and it could risk triggering transatlantic retaliation from the US administration.

    Some may also argue that we already have rules: the Digital Services Act (DSA), they will say, already tackles dark patterns and addictive design. It does not, at least not fully, not for all consumers and not across all digital spaces.

    We need to remember that 97 percent of the most popular apps and websites still use them, so the rules currently in place have not put an end to this online manipulation.

    Concrete demands

    As Socialists & Democrats, we have a clear vision of what a strong DFA can deliver for consumers. Our concrete demands are:

    Ban dark patterns. Things like subscription traps, long click paths to cancel, free trials that turn into paid plans without warning, forced registration, fake other people are viewing this alerts, and items that appear in your basket at checkout should all be prohibited outright.

    Restrict addictive design for all consumers. Features such as endless scrolling should be restricted for everyone, not only children. The bill recently proposed in the Netherlands can serve as an inspiration for Europe.

    Make influencers and the money behind them accountable. Influencers who promote illegal or fraudulent products should be held personally responsible. Commercial deals must be disclosed clearly, not hidden as “#ad” at the end of a hundred hashtags. Those paying influencers also need to be held to account. The products they promote can damage people’s health as well as their finances.

    Put an end to manipulative pricing. Imagine queuing for an ice cream on a sunny Saturday, only to find that it now costs €6 instead of the €3.50 you paid last week – just because it’s hotter and busier. This is unfair pricing, and we want it to be banned in transport, live entertainment, culture and sport. Concerts and matches should not only be for the rich. A car ride should cost the same regardless of your background, your data or your phone’s battery level. People want transparency, but they also want limits, especially in emergency situations, when they are most vulnerable and have no control over the circumstances. 

    Stop gambling-like features in games. Most gamers are adults, not children. Loot boxes and pay-to-win mechanisms should be prohibited so that everyone can play without being manipulated or trapped. This is also a matter of affordability: consumers should not feel forced to buy more than they want to.

    The principle is simple: fairness and safety, by design and by default, should be the rule for every company, whether it runs an app, a social network or an online marketplace. This would also protect the many honest businesses that are undercut today by competitors willing to manipulate their customers.

    At the end of the day, this is also about who holds power online.

    Holding Big Tech companies accountable for how their services shape our behaviour, through surveillance-based ads, harmful content and addictive design, is part of regaining Europe’s digital sovereignty.

    The EU Commission has the evidence, the mandate and our backing. The EU Kids Act, was an important step forward in protecting minors online. Let’s see if Ursula von der Leyen’s executive now shows the same determination to ensure a safer online space for everyone, children and adults alike.

    We will assess the DFA by one test: will it make people’s lives online safer, fairer and more affordable? Consumers should not have to wait any longer to be protected online.

    Reining in Big Tech is a top priority for us, and we’ll be fighting to make sure this legislation protects us all online.

    ]]>         Best way to halt migration is to sabotage Europe’s economy – but nobody wants that, so what are the alternatives? https://euobserver.com/248074/best-way-to-stop-migration-is-to-destroy-europes-economy/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248074 Keeping people impoverished abroad and destroying its economy are Europe's best tools to stop migration. Not even the most anti-migrant politician would seriously push for such a proposal.]]> European policy and law makers have a dilemma. They want to stop irregular migration and deport as many as people as possible.

    But people arriving in Europe irregularly are also lured by work. Spain needs people to pick vegetables and fruit. So does Italy.

    I remember meeting a young man from Bangladesh on the Ocean Viking, freshly rescued after a harrowing night at sea, asking when he would start working in Italy.

    Hein de Haas, a sociologist and university professor in Amsterdam and Maastricht, argues that European labour demand is the ultimate migration driver.

    “By far the best way to stop migration is to destroy your economy,” he recently told Deutsche Welle, a German broadcaster.

    Not even the most anti-migrant politician would seriously push for such a proposal.

    They are instead shoring up controls and restrictions. Some are more obvious than others.

    Bangladesh seems to be a pretty good example. Let me explain.

    ]]>         Watchdog finds patchy customs controls leave big loopholes in EU’s Russia trade sanctions https://euobserver.com/248251/watchdog-finds-patchy-customs-controls-leave-big-loopholes-in-eu-russia-trade-sanctions/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:27:30 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248251 Watchdog finds spotty oversight and unclear rules weaken EU trade sanctions with Russia. Calls on customs authorities and the European Commission to do a better job.]]> When Moscow launched its war against Ukraine in early the 2022, the EU quickly announced sanctions to cripple Russia’s economy.

    Twenty-one sanction packages have since been imposed, designed to punish Russia for its war. In 2021, EU trade with Russia stood at €253bn. Last year, it was €58bn.

    Yet despite EU restrictions, sanctioned trade goods, both imports and exports, still manage to slip into Russia as member states grapple with weak monitoring, spotty enforcement and legal ambiguities.

    This includes everything from dual-use and advanced-technology items found in Russian weapons to industrial goods vital for Russia’s economic and industrial base.

    Of some 202 identified parts in Russian missiles and drones, eight came directly from the EU. Even mundane products like Birch plywood from Russia and Belarus, which get relabelled in a foreign state, end up in the EU market.

    Read more

    In theory it’s from China, in reality it’s from Moscow – how sanctioned Russian timber keeps flowing into Czech Republic

    The findings were part of a larger report on EU sanctions on Russia, by the Luxembourg-based EU watchdog, the European Court of Auditors.

    The court looked at Bulgaria, Germany, Latvia, the Netherlands, and Poland. The differences between the five, in terms of compliance, appears striking.

    The report found Bulgaria recorded no violations of the sanctions. Latvia recorded 2,100. Both share borders with non-EU countries.

EUobserver talks to Patricia Llombart Cussac, the managing director for Africa for the European External Action Service, the EU’s diplomatic corps.]]> “Security in Africa and security in Europe are very much linked. I think we cannot look at the world as we used to look at some few years ago,” says Patricia Llombart Cussac, the managing director for Africa for the European External Action Service, the EU’s diplomatic corps.

    That’s a rebuke to those who think of ‘Fortress Europe’ and would prefer to think of the conflicts in the Horn of Africa and the Middle East as wars in far-flung regions that are of no interest to Europe.

    “This is a completely different vision from the European Union as a donor. This is the European Union as a geopolitical actor. And this is what the relationship we want to continue building with the countries,” she adds.

    Llombart Cussac, a former EU ambassador to Morocco, is hosting a three-day gathering of the EU’s 46 ambassadors across sub-Saharan Africa in Nairobi that started on Tuesday (10 November), where the aim was to reflect on how to strengthen what EU officials call the ‘strategic partnership’ between the bloc and Africa.

    Defence and security partnerships were top of the agenda as well as the bloc’s Global Gateway investment progamme.

    Read more

    EU governments back Global Gateway — but insist Brussels explain where the billions go

    Picking Nairobi was no coincidence, says Llombart Cussac. Kenya is one of the EU’s closest partners in Africa and is a regional hub for east Africa, and also the EU’s diplomatic operations in the region.

    Dynamic cooperation

    Kenya also had a formal defence and security dialogue with the EU earlier in November. Throughout 2026, the EU and Kenya are celebrating the 50 years anniversary of diplomatic relations.

    Security cooperation with Kenya is “a dynamic area of our cooperation,” adds EU ambassador to Kenya, Andreas Peschke.

    ]]>         ‘Made in Europe’ and low-carbon rules up for debate as EU eyes industrial law deal  https://euobserver.com/248217/made-in-europe-and-low-carbon-rules-up-for-debate-as-eu-eyes-industrial-law-deal/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 16:31:48 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248217 EU deputy ambassadors meet on Wednesday to settle which countries count as 'European' and what may count as 'low carbon', as the Irish EU presidency races to strike a deal among member states before the end of the year. ]]> EU deputy ambassadors will on Wednesday (11 November) debate two of the most contested parts of the bloc’s flagship industrial law, which sets “Made in EU” and low-carbon rules for products bought with public money.

    The Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) aims to use public contracts and subsidies to create steady demand for cleaner, European-made industrial products.

    But disagreement over which countries count as ‘European’ has delayed the file. The current Irish EU presidency, which had hoped to get member states on board by late September, is now on its third compromise text and still has no deal.

    A minority of member states led by France want the list kept as short as possible, to steer as much public money as they can towards European companies.

    ]]>         Digital Fairness Act: EU cracks down on influencer ads and manipulative app design https://euobserver.com/248072/digital-fairness-act-eu-cracks-down-on-stealth-influencer-ads-and-manipulative-app-design/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 15:31:08 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248072 The Digital Fairness Act aims to impose stricter protections for people online. While the leaked draft proposes to ban overly-complicated choices to refuse data-sharing, it does not ban addictive design practises outright, warns rights watchdog EDRi. Meanwhile, online retailer Omio have complained that compliance will be costly to businesses.]]> The European Commission is set to unveil new rules on Wednesday (11 November) to prevent people from being manipulated by companies and influencers – but digital rights experts have said the legislation doesn’t go far enough.

    According to a leak of the draft legislation, seen by EUobserver, the Digital Fairness Act (DFA) imposes more controls on how social media influencers can market products, while combatting dark patterns designed to manipulate consumers online.

    In 2022, an EU Commission study found that 97 percent of the most popular websites and apps used by consumers employed dark patterns – intentional design choices to manipulate users towards choices that are more profitable for companies.

    The DFA proposal aims to require that social media influencers state sponsorship deals by prominently labelling advertisements using terms such as “advertisement” or “commercial collaboration”, where influencers cannot misrepresent such adverts as a personal endorsement.

    “People expect that influencers provide genuine advice or tips, not to be quietly sold the latest anti-wrinkle cream or fashionable outfit,” said Agustín Reyna, director general of consumer rights body BEUC. “If someone is promoting products on social media, it should be clearly stated.”

    The draft also proposes a complete ban on misrepresenting information about products, or sending fake message notifications suggesting someone has been in touch when really, nobody messaged.

    “Digital markets have for too long left consumers feeling disempowered and frustrated in a maze of complex cancellation processes for subscriptions they do not want, untransparent ticket pricing, or ‘low stock’ warnings that pressure them,” Reyna added.

    The draft legislation forbids misleading choices about data-sharing or cookies which present refusal as the wrong choice or use deliberately confusing phrases. And the wording of the leaked act also says that cancelling an online subscription should be easy.

    Opt-out for addictive features

    The DFA proposal would only ban personalised advertising and pricing if likely to cause harm and if the consumer is vulnerable.

    And it does not set out to ban addictive features like autoplay or infinite scrolling unless users actively switch off these features.

    “That leaves significant uncertainty and potentially lengthy case-by-case assessments,” said Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, senior policy advisor at rights watchdog EDRi. “Why recognise the problem of addictive design so explicitly without introducing stronger obligations to prevent it?”

    “Offering an opt-out should not automatically be considered sufficient,” she said. 

    Read more

    What is ‘coordinated inauthentic behaviour’ – and how is it distorting Europe’s online democracy?

    However, Domínguez de Olazábal called it a “significant step” that “the commission’s proposal creates binding rules against manipulative design, banning fake message notifications, repeated pressure to reverse choices and deliberately complicated refusal mechanisms.”

    ]]>         As many Russians killed near Pokrovsk in Ukraine as Soviet troops killed in the 1945 Battle of Berlin, according to hacked data (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,720) https://euobserver.com/248106/as-many-russians-killed-near-pokrovsk-in-ukraine-as-soviet-troops-killed-in-the-1945-battle-of-berlin-according-to-hacked-data-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1720/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:56:54 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248106 The data leak reveals a war so costly that battles around Pokrovsk now rival some of the most arrowing clashes of WW2, potentially reshaping how Moscow and Kyiv — as well as their allies — calculate their next moves on the front. ]]>
  • Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers obtained data on dead Russian soldiers from Russia’s statistics agency.
  • Russian data shows 400,000 Russians have been killed in total
  • They show that 74,000 Russian soldiers had been killed in Pokrovsk by December. More Ukrainians, however, died near Robotyne.
  • The brother of Zelensky adviser Mykhailo Podolyak was also killed fighting for Russia.
  • Chart of the day: Number of Ukrainian attacks using Neptune, Flamingo and Storm Shadow missiles.
  • Videos of the day: an attack on the Rubicon base more than 100 km from the front line; an owl fascinated by a drone.

    • Since the start of the invasion of Ukraine, more Russian soldiers have been killed than in all other Soviet and Russian wars since the Second World War combined. This already exceeds the number of US soldiers killed in the Second World War.

    In reality, the war has thus killed at least one percent of Russia’s male population aged 18 to 60.

    This follows from data on the number of Russian soldiers killed, published over the weekend by two hacking groups. The Belarusian pro-opposition group Cyber Partisans and Ukrainian hackers Silent Crow wrote that they had hacked Russia’s statistics agency, Rosstat, and obtained 23 terabytes of data.

    These included records of deaths in Russia in recent years. The data can be used to reconstruct the number of Russian soldiers killed since the beginning of the invasion.

    “In terms of Russian losses, this is the biggest information leak,” German economist Janis Kluge, who researches Russia’s wartime economy and military recruitment, told The Guardian newspaper.

    ]]>         EU Commission to host security talks after week of bomb hoaxes that hit 20 airports and dozens of European flights https://euobserver.com/248019/eu-commission-to-host-security-talks-after-week-of-bomb-hoaxes-that-hit-20-airports-and-dozens-of-european-flights/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:47:21 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248019 Experts from EU member states will meet on Wednesday to discuss last week’s bomb hoaxes affecting dozens of flights across Europe and causing millions in losses.]]> Experts from EU member states will meet on Wednesday (11 November) to discuss last week’s spate of bomb hoaxes which affected dozens of flights across Europe and causing millions in losses.

    The meeting, chaired by the European Commission and also including security experts from non-EU Norway, Switzerland, and Iceland, will serve to review the situation and discuss the need for extra measures.

    At least 35 planes between various airports across Europe faced bomb threats last week, according to Eurocontrol, an organisation for safe air navigation. A Finnair flight between Helsinki and Rome was escorted by Italian fighter jets while another plane, from Dublin to Rome, was diverted to a French air base.

    The scare affected a total of 20 airports in 16 countries, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Serbia, Spain, and the UK.

    The bomb hoaxes affected in total less than 0.5 percent of European flights on any of the three days when alarms were sent, Eurocontrol told EUobserver, and so they “have not had an impact on the delay in the air traffic network.”

    “We remain at full operational readiness,” said EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas last week. “Our priority is clear: the safety of passengers and the smooth functioning of European aviation”.

    Read more

    Fake bomb warnings are hitting European aviation – but the bigger threat came from Jared Kushner

    Though none of the threats turned out to be real, each alarm consumed resources, time, energy, money, and personnel involved, costing €55,000 on average according to media reports, but sometimes reaching even €220,000 per flight affected, according to aviation expert Philippe Baum of Coventry University. This means millions of euros lost across the continent.

    ]]>         The Kraków shooting: A Polish tragedy, a Russian opportunity https://euobserver.com/248113/the-krakow-shooting-a-polish-tragedy-a-russian-opportunity/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:41:57 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248113 As soon as a few images of the perpetrator and the contents of the boot of his car appeared in the media, the Russian propaganda machine was set to work.]]> This may be a hazard of the profession of analysing Russian information warfare, but it is sometimes dazzling to observe how Moscow’s propaganda campaigns are compelled to navigate resonant current affairs and to interpret them – whatever the actual facts – in a light favourable to the Kremlin’s foreign-policy interests.

    This obviously requires a high degree of creativity on the part of Russian propagandists, or suggests to us a boundless space of imagination in which they operate.

    The most tragic events in Poland, where 24-year-old Michał Oksiński killed both of his parents and his sister at home in the town of Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski and then drove to central Kraków and shot dead six people (four Polish nationals, a Briton, and an Austrian), wounding 16 more, offer a case in point.

    As soon as a few images of the perpetrator and the contents of the boot of his car appeared in the media, the Russian propaganda machine was set to work.

    One image showed the perpetrator’s bullet-resistant vest with a patch depicting a modern version of the flag of the early-18th-century pirate Edward Teach, known as “Blackbeard” – a morale patch widely used across the West today.

    Russian propagandists immediately – but wrongly – interpreted the patch as the symbol of the US military lifestyle brand “Forward Observations Group”, whose representatives travelled to Ukraine during the Russian-Ukrainian war.

As the Reagan revolution four decades ago launched US society down the path to low taxes and meager solidarity, perhaps the Republican bloodbath last week could turn US politics toward building a new social contract anchored on an aspiration to equitable prosperity.</p><p>One can sense the ambition of the bumper new crop of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/democrats">Democrats</a> ushered to power last week, calling for support for programs for children and their parents; emphatically endorsing the long-held dream of Medicare for All. The project includes rolling back <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, and restoring subsidies for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act that Republicans allowed to expire. And that’s just the start.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/11/democrats-election-medicaid-costs">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Trump-appointed judge Jeffrey T Kuntz partially denies British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss over edit</p><p>Federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz ruled on Tuesday that Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the BBC can proceed, denying in part the British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss the case.
