      <title>Farewell to Elon Musk’s Cybertruck. Has any car ever been more repellent? | Arwa Mahdawi</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent</link>
      <description><p>Safety campaigners have condemned it and owners have complained about it. Goodbye to a steel monstrosity seemingly designed by a five-year-old</p><p>Elon Musk is having a rough go of it, isn’t he? The world’s richest man spent almost half a billion dollars on the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/04/elon-musk-midterm-spending-analysis">midterms</a> in a failed attempt to defend Republican control of government. Now the tech mogul, who moved from California to Texas to escape Democrats and regulations, finds himself in a newly blue state. He also finds himself the subject of an unflattering <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/08/musk-review-epic-study-worlds-richest-most-banal-man-elon-film">documentary</a> and, if the Democrats follow through on threats to investigate him, could potentially be in a spot of legal bother.</p><p>And to top it all off? Musk’s beloved Cybertruck, the steel monstrosity that looks as if it were designed by a five-year-old, is <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/06/tesla-to-wind-down-cybertruck-production-as-elon-musk-focuses-on-robotics-and-ai">winding down production</a>. According to Musk, this isn’t because it’s an abject failure, but because he is channelling his energy into other things. “This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media,” Musk <a href="https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2119691615774146614?a=pN3ISFVZZ-aU4_-TlJw&amp;s=20">tweeted</a> on Monday. “But rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.” (The Cybercab is a two-passenger robotaxi.)</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comThu, 12 Nov 2026 10:38:12 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Ann Dunne, daughter of Dunnes Stores founder, dies]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/12/ann-dunne-daughter-of-dunnes-stores-founder-dies/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/12/ann-dunne-daughter-of-dunnes-stores-founder-dies/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 10:28:03 +0000Ann Dunne, daughter of Dunnes Stores founder Bernard Dunne, has died.

According to a notice on the RIP.ie website, she died on October 17th peacefully “surrounded by her loving family and friends”, including sister Margaret Heffernan, 84, the current chief executive of Dunnes Stores.

In an accompanying statement, her family said they would like to thank “everyone who has taken care of Ann in her latter years”.

It added that a family funeral has already taken place.

The death of Ann Dunne means Heffernan is now the last remaining child of the late Nora and Bernard Dunne.

Her death has come less than a year after the death of Heffernan’s husband Andrew, who previously worked as a consultant endocrinologist at the Blackrock Clinic.

Ann Dunne is predeceased by her siblings Frank, Elizabeth, Therese and Ben, the latter of whom died in November 2019.

Ben Dunne, who died at the age of 74, played a pivotal role in the expansion of Dunnes Stores, which was set up by his father and grew into the largest retail chain in the country with about 100 stores and a turnover of close to £1 billion at the time of his departure.

He was ousted from the company, which led to his sister Margaret Heffernan taking over, and later built up a chain of well-known gyms.

Heffernan, who has led the supermarket and department store chain since the early 1990s, has been credited with transforming the business into an upmarket retailer during her time in charge.

Following a group restructuring in 2018, the Dunnes Stores group has been controlled through an entity called Better Value Unlimited Company. Due to its unlimited status, the firm is not required to publish financial figures such as turnover and profits.

Better Value Unlimited Company is led by Heffernan and two other directors, her daughter Anne Heffernan and niece Sharon McMahon.

]]>Shawn Williams<![CDATA[Who could run Nvidia if Jensen Huang is ousted?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/12/who-could-run-nvidia-if-jensen-huang-is-ousted/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/12/who-could-run-nvidia-if-jensen-huang-is-ousted/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 10:20:12 +0000Jensen Huang is such a towering figure at Nvidia that his extramarital affairs – with a suspected Chinese spy and reportedly with a colleague – have left the world’s most valuable chipmaker with what could be the world’s biggest corporate succession problem.

Trading on a rags-to-riches life story that saw him make huge, risky long-term bets on the future of the technology market, Huang developed a reputation as a tech visionary whose name was synonymous with – and even eclipsed – that of his company.

Now, in effect for the first time since he cofounded the business in 1993, a true discussion has begun on who might replace him.

“We always knew key man risk was an issue for Nvidia,” said Stacy Rasgon at Bernstein. “It’s not intuitively obvious who the successor would be ... there’s blood in the water now.”

Nvidia employees, known for their fierce loyalty to the chief executive and comparatively low attrition rates, have been left stunned. Some are angry, unsure whether Huang can stay on.

“It’s the biggest fall from grace,” said one long-time Nvidia colleague, adding that a “globally respected and admired” tech group had been brought low “by his own ego and weakness”.

Huang uses an unusual horizontal management structure with about 60 executives reporting directly to him. This gives him enormous reach and influence over every decision made within the company.

The arrangement means that in Huang’s absence, no single executive is positioned to assume his role of chief diplomat, strategist, lobbyist, investor and salesperson. Nor does Nvidia have a formal public succession plan – an idea Huang has said he does not believe in.

Colleagues say Huang is known for dropping into an email thread with relatively junior staff to ask about the minutiae of products. His influence is reflected even in the physical layout of its headquarters.

The chief executive holds court over a large group of executives at the start of each week in a special conference room that doubles as Huang’s office, emphasising the “flat” organisational structure he has developed.

Executives sit around a huge oval desk, with a few rows of stadium-like seating at the back and boards for brainstorming on the walls. “Jensen speaks for most of it,” said one person who has attended these meetings.

That same horizontal system built around a single unique personality is set to fragment if Huang is ousted.

Nvidia’s board, which includes multiple Huang allies who have worked with him since the 1990s, has launched an independent investigation led by a former US federal prosecutor.

One person inside the company said the easiest solution in the event of Huang resigning or being forced out would be for the board to appoint finance chief, Colette Kress, as interim chief executive while it considers a permanent replacement.

The person described Kress – who is well known to the investor and analyst community but has been content to allow her boss to take the limelight – as having the ruthlessness, “sharp elbows” and broad understanding of Nvidia’s sprawling finances needed for the role.

The company has a pipeline of deals and products that stretches into the next decade, meaning there is unlikely to be an immediate impact on its day-to-day operations or strategic roadmap.

Kress, who joined in 2013 from Cisco and who previously worked at Microsoft, is not an engineer like her boss, however, and lacks his technical knowledge. Her first big public test will come on Tuesday when she is due to host the company’s quarterly results call.

Kress is one of an inner circle of four formal executive officers around Huang. The other three are general counsel Tim Teter, operations chief Debora Shoquist and worldwide field operations chief Nick Parker.

Parker joined Nvidia from Microsoft only in August, replacing long-time Huang confidant Jay Puri, who retired. Puri had been overseeing Parker’s transition into that role as “senior adviser”.

Teter, a former lawyer at Palo Alto-based firm Cooley, has played a key role in Nvidia’s lobbying operations over AI chip exports in Washington, which now face a major bipartisan backlash after the midterm elections.

Right now, everyone would benefit from sitting down and taking a few minutes to have a cup of something.

My weekend was largely spent calming people down after last week’s cyberattacks. Supermarket fridges got hacked, there were bomb threats to airlines and the week ended with several media organisations being evacuated due to more bomb threats.

Plenty of otherwise rational people took this as a reason for all-out panic and as a sign of the need to prepare for the end of time. Civilisation isn’t about to collapse and it’s time you had that cuppa.

All of the recent attacks or threats were designed to disrupt. That is in keeping with the experience of countries that previously held the presidency of the Council of the EU.

There was certainly some fiscal impact but the core goal was to cause disorder. Some stock was lost from fridges, some flights were rescheduled and David McCullagh regretted not grabbing his jumper.

Many people became preoccupied with thoughts of, “if the hackers could do this, then what else are they capable of?”.

That’s the wrong question to ask. They are capable of far worse, but you should be asking if doing so is really in their interest.

The big fear I kept hearing about was a national blackout. At their operational best, the most sophisticated hackers could knock out power in Ireland for about 12 hours. Weather is a far more powerful and probable threat to the grid than any malicious actor.

The goal of these disruptions, which are almost always caused by state-backed actors, is to cause fear. It may be Russia today, North Korea tomorrow or the Federated States of Micronesia at the weekend. Instilling fear and uncertainty is a key part of the package.

It probably doesn’t help that these attacks are usually backed up by disinformation campaigns. We need only look at how effective Russia’s disinformation campaign in Poland has been in damaging public support there for Ukraine to see how effective this can be.

The playbook is awfully similar to what we’re seeing here. Some legitimate concerns – which we have had in Ireland following these attacks – are exaggerated to exacerbate fear.

Having a range of goals also works in favour of cybercriminals. Some want to disrupt, some want to stoke fear, others want to steal information or money and quite a few have a cocktail involving elements of all of these. Variety of motive makes it tougher to defend as the method of attack will vary.

No matter what the goal is, it is most unlikely that an all-out attack on Ireland’s core systems is uppermost in the mind of any attackers. The truth is that it does not make sense on a cost-benefit analysis to engage in something at that level.

Attacking the fridges was a good test to see what could be done. Using anonymous accounts to spread bomb threats en masse was a low-to-no-cost means of causing disruption. Taking out the grid or worse? That involves a real commitment and potential blowback. Not from Ireland, oh no, but from those outside Ireland who would be irked.

Multinational data centres and other tech infrastructure here make for tasty targets. Attacking one or a few is certainly a reasonably likely scenario that state-backed cyber attackers will consider. Going for a true shutdown? That gets the Americans angry because it disrupts their businesses. The US government is more than capable of striking back in kind.

Ukraine blowing up three Yandex data centres caused chaos in Moscow. Cyber retaliation by the US government to a cyberattack on their tech giants would make that look like a nosebleed.

Even if the US threat wasn’t there, while Ireland may punch above its weight for its population and economy size, we are far from the juiciest target in the EU, let alone globally.

Besides, with far less risk and at far lower cost, those who caused chaos with our fridges, flights and media last week can get a great return on investment.

They have already got plenty of people afraid. People are fretting about what they might need to do for an improbable attack. Many are realising that they aren’t really capable personally of doing much about it if anything did happen.

Having a torch or a charged power bank is sensible at the best of times. As I said earlier, weather is a real threat to power in this State and winter is coming.

There comes a point where obsessing over being ready for a threat you cannot do much about becomes unhealthy. It doesn’t take long for many people to hit that point.

Between two decades of covering cybersecurity and a lifelong interest in dystopian fiction, I’ve done my share of thinking about worst-case scenarios. Dying carefree beats the hell out of living in fear.

Yes, Ireland had a few mad days of it. It’ll have a few more wild ones in the days and weeks to come but UCD got promoted to football’s top domestic tier and you’ve made yourself a cuppa. Enjoy the good things and relax.

“You may end up paying more in total tax than if you made an outright gift,” says Donnelly.

In transferring the property to his son, the father will be liable for capital gains tax (CGT) as though he were selling it at its full market value of €490,000. This is regardless of whether the transfer is, in part, structured as a loan, says Donnelly.

The father is right. The law will let him use the CGT he owes as a credit against any capital acquisitions tax (CAT) arising for the son. This is because both taxes arise on the same event and the same property, says Donnelly.

A part-gift still qualifies for this offset. However, Revenue practice is to only give credit for the share of the CGT that relates to the gift element – €200,000 in this case.

“That amounts to 200/490ths of the CGT he owes on the property,” says Donnelly.

Also, the credit cannot be more than the CAT the son might owe on the “gifted” element of the property, says Donnelly.

Gift the property outright instead, and the son would have received €67,000 over this tax-free threshold, factoring in the annual small gift exemption of €3,000.

The Government has been repeatedly criticised by the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council and others for failing to adequately budget for things. The €1.2 billion allocation in Budget 2027 for the first year of the public sector pay deal is a case in point. It’s woefully short.

The Government’s latest offer is estimated to cost up to €2 billion next year. One insider said the Coalition had already “blown a hole” through its allocation.

The total cost of the Government’s proposed deal is put at about €4 billion, though, as of now, there are a lot of unknowns on how much will accrue to those on the lower levels of the Civil Service and where backdated element will start from – June or November.

How will it affect the Government’s fiscal position?

The rule of thumb is that each 1 per cent hike in the public sector pay and pensions bill costs the exchequer roughly €370 million.

On that basis, in 2027 the Government’s proposed deal would cost about €1.3 billion on a recurring basis but about €2 billion in cash terms. The €700 million gap reflects the back pay carried over from the previous deal.

So the Government’s fiscal position would be €800 million worse than forecast in 2027. The additional pay bumps for 2028 and 2029 are also not factored in. That additional money will have to come out of tax resources and will reduce the Government’s budget surpluses over the period.

On the other side of the ledger, the State’s financial position is expected to be boosted by corporate tax receipts, which are predicted to rise to €45 billion by 2030.

Either way, the State will be wrapping more day-to-day spending into potentially risky tax receipts.

How does the Government offer compare with what private sector workers are getting?

The Government’s recent economic and fiscal outlook, published alongside last month’s budget, forecast that wages across the economy – which is mainly private sector – would rise by 4.1 per cent in 2027 and by 3.7 per cent in 2028 and 2029.

The Government’s 10.5 per cent deal gives public sector workers a 3-3.5 per cent bump in pay across those years, according to one estimate. On that basis, the hikes are roughly comparable.

Private sector wages have outpaced those in the public sector since 2008. According to the official data, private sector wages are up by between 52-56 per cent over that period versus 25 per cent in the public sector.

Private sector wage growth data is skewed by multinationals that pay their workers significantly more than the average. That said, tech companies in Ireland have been pruning their wage bill.

What is the likelihood of unions accepting the deal?

Workers are in the midst of a nasty cost-of-living shock, compounded by an energy price surge. Meanwhile, the Government is attempting to rein in spending that has been something of a runaway train since the pandemic. Hence the fraught atmosphere around these negotiations.

Minister for Finance Simon Harris said the Coalition’s ability to offer income tax cuts in the recent budget and increases in public sector wages was in stark contrast to many other European governments, which were short on money and facing “extraordinarily difficult” economic decisions.

Trade unions insist, however, that the surge in inflation has severely degraded the purchasing power of their members, particularly those earning €50,000 or less, and must be addressed. They also insist there are acute labour shortages in education and healthcare and argue that a lacklustre deal will worsen the exodus of young nurses and teachers.

With more industrial action looming, a breakthrough needs to come quickly.

]]>Sinenkiy<![CDATA[Is the European Union getting real about ending tech dependence?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/11/11/is-the-european-union-getting-real-about-ending-tech-dependence/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/11/11/is-the-european-union-getting-real-about-ending-tech-dependence/Wed, 11 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000

Europeans are afraid – very afraid – of their dependence on foreign digital technology.

A recent poll by the Bertelsmann Foundation finds almost three-quarters of European Union (EU) citizens worry that critical digital services “could be remotely disabled by actors outside Europe”. The same overwhelming majority think it important Europe should have “control over key digital technologies”.

As in other cases (such as Europeans’ negative reactions to the EU trade “deal” with Donald Trump last year), the bloc’s citizens are clear about what they want – and it’s not what they are getting at the moment. So how are European governments, and the EU in particular, going about delivering the “control” that voters demand?

Europe depends on other economies for much of the digital technology “stack”: the US for software, Taiwan for microchips, China for swathes of hardware. A first question, then, is how much of the stack needs to be home-grown inside the EU.

When I ask this of Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission vice-president in charge of tech sovereignty, she lists AI (artificial intelligence) models, semiconductors, quantum technology, satellites and the cloud as areas where Europe needs its own productive capacity. She does not go as far as self-sufficiency; the objective is “that we shouldn’t have risky dependencies [or be] dependent on one company or one third country”.

That is an ambitious list of sectors nonetheless, given how far behind Europe is. It is certainly sufficiently demanding that we must ask whether pursuing it would come at the cost of falling further behind and of giving up foreign frontier technology for the sake of inferior home-made versions. What does Brussels think about that trade-off?

US voters have rejected data centres and AI. What happens now?

It may not be that dramatic, Virkkunen suggests. “Sometimes we know that some companies ... want to give the impression that they always have the best services and the competitors don’t ... and it’s not always true,” she tells me.

She argues that the home-grown alternatives are sometimes just smaller and lesser known, rather than uncompetitive on quality or price. But that means the public sector can catalyse domestic substitutes by playing its role as a customer right.

Is the European public sector doing that, though? Many smaller EU-based digital companies feel they have a good product but government customers prefer to stick with the big providers they are used to. The commissioner accepts there is a degree of inertia. There is also a need to be “creative”, she says, to facilitate smaller companies coming together in consortiums to provide the scale of supply needed.

The biggest challenge, though, is access to funding for EU tech companies – not because of a lack of savings but thanks to Europe’s failure to channel financing to risky ventures. EU institutions as well as member states are starting to remedy this: a new scale-up fund is now operational and Brussels aims for more public-sector strategic “anchor” equity to crowd in private investors.

But so far the amounts being mobilised seem far too small compared to the hundreds of billions put into US tech investments every year. And by all accounts, talks over the EU’s next multiyear budget are whittling down further the amounts Brussels had originally proposed for new priorities including digital industrial policy.

On legislative reforms, too, from “EU Inc” (a pan-EU corporate entity) to localisation rules for sensitive digital services, member states are delaying or watering down proposals where Brussels already seemed to have been cautious not to ask for too much.

Virkkunen naturally avoids criticising national capitals. But she agrees that in the budget talks, “it’s very important that the member states keep the ambition there” for funding new technologies and defence. And not just to build domestic capacity, but because “the idea is that they should be able to compete globally”.

Ultimately, Brussels, while ambitious, seems to be aiming somewhere in between how far voters want to go and how far national governments are ready to move.

That means there are political rewards to be had for leaders bold enough to go further and faster. In the Bertelsmann poll, less than half of those asked think foreign providers are successfully held to European rules and expectations. It’s now up to politicians to convince them otherwise. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

The average car insurance premium last year was €655, an increase of €144 in just three years. But you don’t have to accept another expensive renewal.

Actuaries know exactly what insurers look for when calculating a premium. Understanding their secrets could help you get a cheaper quote. Here are 10 tips to save on your next policy.

1. Check your mileage

Which drivers present the highest risk? Those who spend the most time on the road. One of the best predictors of a car crash is how much time you spend driving, says actuary Noel Garvey, who is chairman of the Society of Actuaries’ general insurance committee.

That’s why insurers ask your estimated annual mileage when quoting for your policy.

“The more you drive, the higher the chance of an accident,” says Garvey. More mileage means more risk, so insurers will charge you more.

Close to one million people reported working from home at least sometimes in the second quarter of 2026, according to Central Statistics Office (CSO) figures. If you are one of them, tell your insurer.

The average private car in Ireland covered 15,196km in 2023, according to the CSO. Many people drive less.

To check your mileage, divide the odometer reading by the car’s age in years, says Motorcheck.ie. Or check the readings between NCT certificates, work out the difference in mileage and compare it to the national average.

Overestimating your mileage when seeking a quote means paying more than you need to. But you need to play fair. Underestimating to save money could cause problems if you need to claim.

Why is motor insurance so expensive in Ireland?

2. Excess

You don’t have to be an actuary to get a better price on car insurance but it pays to know more about how your quote is designed, says Garvey.

Ask your insurer how the price changes if you increase the excess, he says. This is the amount you agree to pay towards a claim. It’s often set at a default of €250 to €300.

If there’s a crash and you submit a claim for €4,000 and your policy excess is €200, for example, you’ll pay the first €200 and the insurance company will pay €3,800.

Agreeing to a higher excess could mean a cheaper quote.

“If you back yourself to be more careful than most, it might be well worth taking on that risk,” says Garvey.

Just ensure the excess you set is affordable in case of a mishap.

What are telematics policies, and how can they knock thousands off motor insurance costs?

Price comparison website bonkers.ie sought quotes from a range of providers, including AIG, Aviva and Zurich, under a number of conditions and found that a 20-year-old driver with a full licence could get a quote of just €570 for fully comprehensive telematics cover.

When there was no telematics cover, the price of the standard policy jumped to almost €3,900.

How common are car fires?

6. Drop to one car

If your household has two cars and one spends most of its time sitting in the drive, dropping to one car will save you thousands.

Typically, in a two-car household both members have “main driver” status on their respective policies, with individual no-claims bonus records. You probably have “named driver” cover on each other’s policies too.

EV public charging costs now exceeding those for petrol and diesel

Polestar’s future-gazing new concept is far more rational than it appears

8. Pay annually

Paying for your car insurance in instalments can ease the blow to your monthly budget, but this can mean extra charges.

“The total paid over the year may be higher than the headline annual premium,” says Garvey. “Look at the overall cost, not just the monthly instalment when comparing quotes.”

Pay the yearly amount upfront if you can, even if that means dipping into your savings, or start to put a little bit of money away each month now so that you can pay in full next year, says Mabs.

9. Don’t modify

Thinking of buying a modified car or modifying your own? Engine modifications, changes to the wheels, suspension or bodywork can all drive up your quote.

“Modifications can affect an insurer’s assessment of the vehicle’s risk, value or likely repair cost, so you should disclose them and check the potential insurance impact before making changes,” says Garvey.

Boy racers take note.

10. Shop around

Automatically renew your policy with your existing insurer and you will pay more. Too many of us do this: maybe that’s why net profit among Irish motor insurers hit €89 million last year.

You’ll need details of any claims in the past five years too. You’ll find those in your current policy documents.

If you are shopping around by phone, ask if it’s cheaper for you to complete the transaction online. Many insurers provide an online discount.

And if there is more than one car in your household, ask your insurer for a multipolicy discount.

]]><![CDATA[Cork solicitor due to retire this week prohibited from practising by High Court]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/cork-solicitor-due-to-retire-this-week-prohibited-from-practice-by-high-court/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/cork-solicitor-due-to-retire-this-week-prohibited-from-practice-by-high-court/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:22:55 +0000A Cork solicitor has been prohibited by the High Court from practising even though he has indicated to the Law Society he is going to retire this week and close his office.

This came after the Legal Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal last year made two findings of misconduct against Moylan.

This followed an inquiry into allegations that the solicitor had failed to take any adequate steps to register an enduring power of attorney for an elderly man in a nursing home or to reply adequately or at all to correspondence or phone calls from a member of the man’s family.

In an affidavit to the court, Antony Watson, LSRA head of complaints, investigations and resolutions, said the tribunal considered the sanction necessary to protect the public, maintain the reputation of the solicitors’ profession, to punish Moylan and to discourage him and other members of the profession from repeating or emulating the misconduct.

High Court president Judge David Barniville said he was satisfied that the sanction was appropriate and proportionate.

Moylan will also have to pay €1,500 as restitution to the woman who had complained that the solicitor had failed to register an enduring power of attorney for her grandfather.

Moylan (72), who has been a solicitor for 48 years, has indicated he is to retire on Friday this week and was liaising with the Law Society in relation to a wind-down of his practice, the court heard.

Earlier, during a separate application by the Law Society, the judge was told that Moylan had indicated he intended to retire from the practice this week, but the Law Society needed an order from the court so it could take control of the solicitor’s practice and facilitate an orderly wind-down.

Moylan was consenting to the orders sought. The judge said he was satisfied the orders sought were appropriate.

On the LSRA matter before the court, Watson in his affidavit said the tribunal held an inquiry into two allegations in relation to the complaint.

Watson said Moylan indicated that he admitted the facts. He had been instructed by a man in the summer of 2020 to prepare an enduring power of attorney. It was to be registered when the man lost capacity. Moylan was informed in July 2022 that the man had lost capacity and the solicitor was asked by his granddaughter to register the enduring power of attorney.

Moylan failed to reply adequately or at all to correspondence from the man’s granddaughter or to return her calls and emails sent between August 2022 and December 2022, it was claimed.

The woman gave evidence to the inquiry about her grandfather’s declining health and the need to discharge his nursing home bills.

Watson said the tribunal found the allegations were proven as to fact and “proven as to misconduct being an act or omission connected with the provision by the solicitor of legal services which were to a substantial degree of an inadequate standard”.

He said the tribunal gave its reasons for making the recommendations before the High Court, including that the findings of misconduct were serious and went to the protection of the public. While the tribunal gave credit to Moylan for his admissions as to fact, it was of the opinion that his insight was limited.

It also noted Moylan had been practising for a long period, had no finding of misconduct until 2022 and was close to retirement.

Moylan’s previous disciplinary history, Watson said, was considered by the tribunal as an aggravating factor. The tribunal did not recommend suspension because Moylan was close to retirement and intended to wind down his practice.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[DCC takes £348.3m charge against tech unit before sale deal]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/dcc-takes-3483m-charge-against-tech-unit-before-sale-deal/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/dcc-takes-3483m-charge-against-tech-unit-before-sale-deal/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 15:53:57 +0000DCC Energy booked a £348.3 million (€416.9 million) charge against its technology unit in the six months to the end of September as it neared a deal to sell the business.

The impairment charge pushed DCC into a net loss of £323.7 million for the period, according to its latest financial results, published on Tuesday.

The Dublin-based group, which is in the process of being taken over by US private equity firms KKR and Energy Capital Partners, said in early October that it will receive $701 million (€626.8 million) in net proceeds for the tech unit, called Nexora, which it has agreed to sell to New York-based One Equity Partners.

KKR and Energy Capital had promised as part of their deal to give DCC shareholders a £1.25-a-share payout if Nexora achieved $800 million. That was in addition to £65.25-a-share on offer for the wider group. The company’s shareholders will have to make do with a third of the £1.25 maximum additional consideration.

The deal was also well below that some analysts had initially expected the division to achieve when DCC chief executive Donal Murphy announced in late 2024 that the group was abandoning what remained of its conglomerate roots to focus on energy.

“Following the agreement to dispose of [Nexora] in October 2026, a non-cash impairment before tax of £348.3 million has been recognised in the current period to reflect the expected proceeds on disposal,” DCC said on Tuesday.

“The net charge also includes restructuring, redundancy and transaction-related costs associated with the disposal and separation of the business, and a gain of £12.7 million on the disposal of property in North America. There was a related tax credit of £24.4 million in relation to these charges.”

DCC confirmed that it expects the Nexora sale to be completed by March 1st and the KKR and Energy Capital takeover to be finalised “in the first quarter” of 2027.

]]>Nick Bradshaw for The Irish Times<![CDATA[Cost of residential land in Dublin nearly triple national median]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/cost-of-residential-land-in-dublin-nearly-triple-national-median/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/cost-of-residential-land-in-dublin-nearly-triple-national-median/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 13:02:59 +0000Residentially zoned land in Dublin commanded nearly three times the price paid for land in other parts of the country last year, according to the Central Statistics Office (CSO).

The median, or middle value, price paid for an acre of residential development land in Dublin in 2025 was €721,288.

This compared with a national median price of €258,716.

Land in Dublin and its commuter counties typically commands a premium because of the population concentration.

Dublin and the southwest region – Cork and Kerry – had the highest median prices per acre in 2025, at €721,288 and €469,061, respectively.

The Border region had the lowest regional median, at €122,300 per acre.

By county, Kerry had the highest published median price per acre in 2025, at €727,053, followed by Dublin at €721,288 and Galway at €470,723.

However, the Kerry figure appears to have been inflated by a small number of high-value transactions.

Leitrim had the lowest published county median, at €71,894 per acre

The value of residential land sold last year amounted to €217.9 million, the CSO said.

The greatest recorded volume of land sold was in the mideast – Kildare, Louth, Meath and Wicklow – at 103.3 acres. The midlands recorded the lowest volume, at 24.6 acres.

The CSO noted that the value and volume of transactions included in its release did not represent all residentially zoned land sales. “Only transactions where the land area could be verified at the time of sale are included,” it said.

Individuals accounted for more than two-thirds – 72.3 per cent – of vendors by number of transactions in 2025, while construction companies accounted for 68.5 per cent of the value of land purchased.

Construction companies bought just a third of the land sold for housing last year

In 2025, land subject to the residentially zoned land tax had a median price per acre of €329,896, compared with €184,421 for land not subject to the tax, a difference of about 79 per cent.

“This is a descriptive comparison and does not establish that the tax caused the price difference,” the agency said.

The latest snapshot of house prices from the CSO will be published next week. It is expected to show that the market here is cooling with purchasing power impacted by higher borrowing costs.

The latest numbers for the month of August put inflation (for prices paid) at 5.1 per cent and at 3.9 per cent in Dublin.

The CSO’s numbers are based on stamp duty data from Revenue and reflect transactions that took place at least two months ago; as a result there is a lag.

The Irish property market is undergoing something of a reset in the face of higher borrowing costs, persistent supply shortages and changes to the rental rules.

]]>Francesco Scatena<![CDATA[At Web Summit opener, Palestine gets a brief mention and the loudest cheer]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/at-web-summits-opener-palestine-gets-a-brief-mention-and-the-loudest-cheer/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/at-web-summits-opener-palestine-gets-a-brief-mention-and-the-loudest-cheer/Mon, 09 Nov 2026 20:14:16 +0000Paddy Cosgrave welcomed thousands of Web Summit early arrivals to Lisbon on Monday night, telling them the future of technology was “increasingly Chinese”, with “more than 50 superstars from China’s leading AI labs” attending the technology conference.

]]>Patricia De Melo Moreira<![CDATA[Situation ‘grim’ after State-backed medtech start-up suffered delays bringing products to market]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/situation-grim-after-state-backed-medtech-start-up-suffered-delays-bringing-products-to-market/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/situation-grim-after-state-backed-medtech-start-up-suffered-delays-bringing-products-to-market/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 12:38:35 +0000The situation at an Enterprise Ireland-backed medtech firm last year was “very grim” after delays in bringing its products to market, with shareholders warning that funding might not be forthcoming, its chief executive has said.

“I couldn’t work under the enforced conditions. I was facing severe financial difficulties; the contract was already void,” Ul Ahad said.

]]>Eric Luke<![CDATA[Competition watchdog to target ‘bid rigging’ for National Development Plan projects ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/competition-watchdog-plans-focus-on-national-development-plan-project-bid-rigging/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/competition-watchdog-plans-focus-on-national-development-plan-project-bid-rigging/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 10:16:01 +0000Billions of taxpayer euro could be saved on National Development Plan projects by tougher enforcement of competition law, according to the State’s competition watchdog.

Cabinet on Tuesday approved a three-year strategy submitted by the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC), which oversees mergers and acquisitions, consumer protection and commercial competition.

It lists tackling the risk of bid rigging, where contenders secretly agree on which one of them should win a contract, as one of the commission’s “key areas of focus” as the Government prepares to spend €275 billion overhauling the State’s infrastructure.

CCPC chairman Brian McHugh says international experience shows that, with public procurement on this scale, the potential cost to taxpayers of bid rigging could run to hundreds of millions of euro if not billions, he says. “That is the scale of harm that’s out there.”

Discussing the proposed strategy, McHugh says the CCPC has the powers to tackle cartels and is keen to use them. “We really want to take on as many cases as possible but the reality is that will take resources. The more resources we have, the more cases we will take [on].”

Cartels, where businesses agree not to compete with each other in a given market, could be responsible for up 20 or 30 per cent of price increases on projects, McHugh notes.

The commission says it already has a “healthy pipeline of cases” but its chairman cautions that these investigations take time. Big companies have the right to challenge those investigations and any subsequent sanctions, and they have the financial resources to do so.

The commission has got extra resources from Government as its task has become more complex, including 56 more staff over the life of its previous strategy.

On consumer protection, McHugh says the CCPC is acutely aware of the impact of rising energy prices and the likelihood of food-price inflation on households. The commission continues to monitor both areas closely but he is comfortable that rising grocery prices here are “not the result of a dysfunctional market”.

The CCPC has reviewed grocery prices in Ireland several times in recent years, finding that the State has one of the lowest rates of food inflation in Europe. McHugh says that is largely the result of the presence of discounters in the Irish market.

“We will continue to keep an eye on them,” he says of fuel and food prices. “We never give any market a clean bill of health.”

Reviews are intended to highlight areas where reforms would benefit consumers. Currently, the CCPC is looking at pharmacies with a report due next year.

“Obviously it’s an important market, every family uses pharmacies,” McHugh observes. But it is also a complicated market in relation to how prices are set and how consumers end up going from their doctor to a particular pharmacy. “That’s something we want to understand,” he says.

Key issues include how pharmacies compete with each other in those circumstances and how consumers can shop around. What kind of information is available to them.

McHugh hopes the Oireachtas will pass legislation next year giving the CCPC the power to fine businesses for breaking consumer protection rules, as it already can do for competition law breaches.

Currently, these cases go to the District Court, which generally orders them to make a €1,000 contribution. Under the proposed administrative regime, the CCPC will decide on its own fines.

In doing so, the regulator would take account of the offence, the size of the market, how many consumers were affected, the level of harm inflicted on them and whether the company had previously broken the law, McHugh says.

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3447399/">
   <title>Andacht in der Mehrzweckhalle</title>
   <description>Die Musiklegende Bob Dylan macht für drei Konzerte in Österreich Station. Bereits bei seinem ersten Auftritt am Mittwochabend in der Wiener Stadthalle begeisterte und irritierte der 85-jährige Altmeister seine Anhängerinnen und Anhänger gleichermaßen. Denn kaum ein Künstler weiß mit Erwartungen so zu spielen wie der US-Amerikaner. Für das drei Generationen umspannende Publikum wurde der Abend zur emotionalen und gelungenen Andacht des Abschiednehmens.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3447950/">
   <title>Druck auf Nvidia-Chef Huang steigt</title>
   <description>Bei Nvidia könnte sich laut Medienberichten schon bald die Zukunft von Firmenchef Jensen Huang entscheiden. Der langjährige Chef des weltweit führenden Anbieters von Chips für künstliche Intelligenz (KI) geriet wegen einer außerehelichen Affäre mit einer mutmaßlichen chinesischen Spionin unter Druck. Medienberichten zufolge sei eine weitere Affäre aufgeflogen. Nun drohe Huang der Rauswurf, hieß es mit Verweis auf eine mit der Sache vertraute Person.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3447886/">
   <title>Streit über weitere Ukraine-Hilfen</title>
   <description>Gleich zwei europäische Gipfeltreffen in Dublin beschäftigen sich diese Woche mit dem weiteren Beistand für die Ukraine. Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU kommen am Donnerstag zunächst auf dem Gipfel der Europäischen Politischen Gemeinschaft (EPG) zusammen. Hier nehmen neben den 27 EU-Ländern noch rund 20 weitere Staaten teil. Am Freitag steht dann der informelle EU-Gipfel in der irischen Hauptstadt an. Kurz vor den Gipfeltreffen entbrannte erneut ein heftiger Streit über die künftige Unterstützung für die Ukraine.</description>
   <link>https://orf.at/stories/3447886/</link>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3447947/">
   <title>Demokrat erobert Senatssitz in Mississippi</title>
   <description>Die republikanische US-Senatorin Cindy Hyde-Smith hat laut US-Medien das Senatsrennen im traditionell konservativen US-Bundesstaat Mississippi gegen den Demokraten Scott Colom verloren. Kurz nach dem Sender CNN erklärten am Mittwoch auch andere Medien, darunter der Sender NBC und die Nachrichtenagentur AP, Colom zum Sieger. Hyde-Smith räumte in der Folge ihre Niederlage ein. Colom wird der erste demokratische Senator in über 40 Jahren sowie der erste schwarze Senator in dem Südstaat seit den 1880er Jahren.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3447888/">
   <title>Generalstreik in Zeiten politischer Spannung</title>
   <description>In Spanien hat am Mittwoch ein Generalstreik gegen die Wohnungskrise das öffentliche Leben und die Wirtschaft zum Teil lahmgelegt. Es war der erste ganztägige Generalstreik im Land seit 14 Jahren. Die beiden großen Gewerkschaften sahen einen Erfolg, Arbeitgebervertreter übten Kritik. Der Streik fand in Zeiten politischer Spannungen statt, schließlich steht Spanien unmittelbar vor der heißen Phase des Wahlkampfs.</description>

Notes From Poland https://notesfrompoland.com regular summaries of news from Poland Thu, 12 Nov 2026 08:41:00 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9 https://notesfrompoland.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/cropped-2019-10-29_1838-32x32.png Notes From Poland https://notesfrompoland.com 32 32 Polish deputy foreign minister charged over alleged misappropriation of millions of zloty https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/12/polish-deputy-foreign-minister-charged-over-alleged-misappropriation-of-millions-of-zloty/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 08:30:00 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106632

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

A Polish deputy foreign minister has been charged with misappropriating millions of zloty entrusted to him and taking steps to prevent creditors from recovering money owed to them.

Prosecutors say that Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski used the money for personal expenses and to buy three apartments in Warsaw. His wife has also been charged in the case. Both of them deny the allegations, and Bartoszewski says he “will defend the truth and my good name”.

Prokurator z mazowieckiego wydziału PZ PK przedstawił posłowi na Sejm RP Władysławowi Teofilowi Bartoszewskiemu dwa zarzuty: przywłaszczenia powierzonych mu środków pieniężnych znacznej wartości oraz udaremnienia zaspokojenia wierzyciela.

Komunikat: ➡️ https://t.co/EXZ3NsovBh pic.twitter.com/Lmp2f3Bw2r

— Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) November 10, 2026

The case dates back to before Bartoszewski had entered politics. In 2019, he became an MP for the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL). In 2023, after PSL became a junior partner in the current ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk, he was made deputy foreign minister.

From 2004, say prosecutors, Bartoszewski was entrusted with managing the assets of Polish art collector and philanthropist Andrzej Ciechanowiecki, who was Bartoszewski’s godfather and a friend of his late father, Władysław Bartoszewski, a former Polish resistance fighter, Auschwitz prisoner, and later foreign minister.

From 2005, Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski, who has waived his right to anonymity in the case, also managed funds belonging to the Non Omnis Moriar Foundation, linked to the collector.

According to prosecutors, Bartoszewski used some of the money to buy and renovate three apartments in Warsaw between 2005 and 2006. From 2009, Ciechanowiecki began asking Bartoszewski to account for the funds, but he allegedly failed to do so and began avoiding contact with Ciechanowiecki.

 

In 2012, Ciechanowiecki and the foundation terminated their agreements with Bartoszewski and demanded the return of funds, say prosecutors. The following year, they filed a lawsuit demanding that Bartoszewski pay them around £1 million, 7.2 million zloty, €650,000 and $76,000, plus interest.

According to prosecutors, Bartoszewski then took steps to prevent the money from being recovered. A company owned by him and his wife sold three apartments in Warsaw, after which the couple disposed of their shares in the company. His wife also donated a property to their underage children.

“As a result of these actions, Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski and his wife possess no assets from which the creditor’s claims could be satisfied,” prosecutors said.

In March 2024, a Warsaw court ordered Bartoszewski to pay the foundation more than 13.2 million zloty, plus interest. Prosecutors note that the judgment is not yet binding as an appeal is still pending.

Od półtora roku sąd nie wyznaczył terminu apelacji w sprawie Władysława Teofila Bartoszewskiego — dowiedział się Onet. Sąd pierwszej instancji nakazał wiceministrowi spraw zagranicznych zwrot aż 13 mln zł, jakie powierzył mu jego chrzestny https://t.co/JzPwcJG4KU

— Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) November 4, 2025

Meanwhile, in 2023, representatives of the Ciechanowiecki Collection Foundation at the Royal Castle in Wawel, which now holds the assets of Ciechanowiecki (who died in 2015), filed a notification to prosecutors of alleged crimes committed by Bartoszewski and his wife.

Earlier this year, the prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, asked parliament to lift Bartoszewski’s immunity so that prosecutors could bring charges against him. However, he voluntarily waived it on 6 October.

At the time, Bartoszewski told newspaper Fakt that he “absolutely does not feel guilty” and “the evidence confirms this”. He also claimed that there is “a political element to my case”, though he did not elaborate further.

Sejmowa komisja regulaminowa opowiedziała się we wtorek za uchyleniem immunitetu posła PSL Władysława Teofila Bartoszewskiego w związku z wnioskiem prokuratury w sprawie podejrzenia popełnienia przez niego między innymi przestępstwa przywłaszczenia mienia.https://t.co/ydA0jNNUQ8

— tvn24 (@tvn24) October 6, 2026

On Tuesday this week, prosecutors announced that they had charged Bartoszewski with misappropriation of funds of significant value – £1 million, €405,000 and 6,683,705 zloty – entrusted to him by Ciechanowiecki and the foundation. The offence carries a prison sentence of between one and 10 years.

A second charge concerns allegedly taking steps to prevent or reduce the recovery of money owed to a creditor. It carries a prison sentence of between three months and five years.

Prosecutors say that, on the same day, they “brought similar charges” against Bartoszewski’s wife and that both of the accused denied guilt.

Wiceszef MSZ Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski oświadczył, że nie przyznaje się do popełnienia zarzucanych mu przez prokuraturę czynów. Zapowiedział, że będzie bronił prawdy i swojego dobrego imienia "tak długo, jak będzie to konieczne". https://t.co/tGodfs9Gzi

— Interia (@Int_Wydarzenia) November 10, 2026

In a statement issued later on Tuesday, Bartoszewski issued a statement rejecting the allegations and saying that he “will defend the truth and my good name in every instance, for as long as necessary”, reports the Polish Press AGency (PAP).

“I am convinced that both the criminal proceedings and the ongoing civil proceedings will confirm my arguments and rights to my property,” he added.

“I consistently maintain that all actions related to the acquisition of the real estate were consistent with the original will of Andrzej Ciechanowiecki expressed at the time of their purchase, and the premises were intended to constitute permanent financial security for my family.”

Asked whether the prime minister would dismiss Bartoszewski following the charges or wait for a court ruling, government spokesperson Adam Szłapka said that the deputy minister “is currently on leave and decisions regarding this matter will be made upon his return”.

]]> Annual Polish Independence March passes through Warsaw https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/11/annual-polish-independence-march-passes-through-warsaw/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 15:34:34 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106667

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The annual march held in Warsaw to mark Poland’s Independence Day has passed through the city without major incident. This year’s event took place amid heightened security following the deadly terrorist attack in Kraków just four days earlier.

Hundreds of thousands of people, including President Karol Nawrocki, marched through the city amid a sea of white-and-red flags. The event, which is organised by nationalist groups, also acted as a display of unity among the right-wing and far-right opposition ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections.

Figures from the more liberal government, as always, avoided the march. Prime Minister Donald Tusk celebrated Independence Day hundreds of kilometres away in the city of Szczecin, where he issued an invitation to the opposition-aligned Nawrocki to visit his home for talks.

Zapełnia się rondo im. Romana Dmowskiego. Cała transmisja z #marszuniepodległości w @TV_Trwam pic.twitter.com/TvMHypx8gn

— Michał Rybka (@_MRybka) November 11, 2026

This year’s Independence March was held under the slogan “Polak w Polsce gospodarzem”, which translates roughly as “Poles are in charge in their own country”.

The slogan was chosen to “emphasise our opposition to foreign influences on Poland and underscore that Poland should be a nation-state without mass immigration”, said Rafał Buca, the march’s spokesman. “In Poland, Poles should rule – not some foreigners, not the European Union, not big corporations.”

On the morning of the march, the organisers shared an image showing Tusk as a puppet of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. “Time to cut the strings of foreign influence,” they declared.

Czas odciąć sznurki obcych wpływów i marionetkowych decyzji!

W naszym własnym kraju to my – polscy obywatele – jesteśmy jedynym suwerenem i to my ustalamy reguły!

🇵🇱 POLAK W POLSCE GOSPODARZEM! pic.twitter.com/8Htr8s0klx

— Marsz Niepodległości (@StowMarszN) November 11, 2026

The main organisers of the march are associated with Confederation (Konfederacja), a far-right group that sits among the opposition in parliament. But it is attended by a wide range of people, from the mainstream right through to the radical right.

Leading figures from other opposition parties, including the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), centre-right Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) and radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), were present, as well as Nawrocki, who last year became the first Polish president to attend the march.

A member of the march’s organising committee, Marcin Osowski, told broadcaster WNET that around half a million people were at today’s event. The municipal authorities, which are under the control of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, later put the figure at around 250,000.

That would make today’s Independence March the largest ever other than the one in 2018, when a broader event was organised to mark the centenary of Poland regaining its independence after World War One.

 

The opposition was aiming to show a united front amid their ongoing protests against the recent takeover of the constitutional court by a group of government-backed judges and ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections, at which they hope to unseat Tusk’s government.

“It’s about showing our strength and, at the same time, for this march to be a springboard for the election campaign,” said Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of PIS, during the march, quoted by the Niezależna news website. “Unity is important.”

Meanwhile, one of the leaders of Confederation, Krzysztof Bosak, told the crowd in a speech that, “while we have different experiences and views, under the white-and-red flag we form one community”.

“Next year, we must turn this community into an election victory…We must remove the current clique from power and form a pro-Polish government,” he declared. “We do not accept the violent takeover of state institutions. We demand respect for the law.”

Na Marszu Niepodległości jesteśmy u siebie! Przyjeżdżamy z różnych stron, mamy różne doświadczenia i poglądy, ale pod biało-czerwoną flagą tworzymy jedną wspólnotę. Każdy jest w niej potrzebny. Także ten, kto dziś czuje się samotny, odrzucony i traci poczucie sensu.

Ta wspólnota… pic.twitter.com/L5pYU1RVv0

— Krzysztof Bosak 🇵🇱 (@krzysztofbosak) November 11, 2026

However, Confederation’s other main leader, Sławomir Mentzen, shared a picture of himself at the march in front of a banner showing images of both Tusk and Kaczyński crossed out, alongside the word “Reset”.

While Bosak’s nationalist faction of Confederation is seen as more amenable to the idea of working with PiS to form a potential future coalition government, Mentzen’s libertarian faction is less enthusiastic about the idea.

Nadchodzi, nadchodzi Marsz Niepodległości! 🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/o8Tkf8673G

— Sławomir Mentzen (@SlawomirMentzen) November 11, 2026

In the past, the march has sometimes seen violence, with participants clashing with police. However, in recent years it has generally passed peacefully, and that was again the case today.

The city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaszkowski, who is a deputy leader of KO, said on Wednesday afternoon that, other than the illegal use of pyrotechnics (such as a flare held up by Mentzen), the march was proceeding without incident.

Local authorities in Warsaw had put in place additional security measures following Saturday’s terrorist attack in Kraków, in which a 24-year-old Polish man, Michał Oksiński, killed six people and injured over a dozen more by shooting an AR-15 rifle from his car.

Oksiński’s rampage was quickly brought to a halt in a shootout with armed police, and he died from his injuries on Monday. On Tuesday, the justice minister revealed that evidence uncovered so far shows “strong traces of right-wing extremism” in Oksiński’s activity.

There are "strong traces of right-wing extremism" in the activity of the man who carried out the mass shooting in Kraków, says Poland's justice minister.

His search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist https://t.co/UhVbkWSaCq

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026

Tusk, meanwhile, celebrated Independence Day in the city of Szczecin in northwest Poland.

“All of us, without exception, are responsible for ensuring that Poland remains strong, secure, free and independent forever,” said the prime minister. “Everyone who holds Poland in their hearts must understand that independence, freedom and a secure republic are a common good.”

Tusk noted that, since the recent crisis around the constitutional court broke out, Nawrocki has refused his offer to meet and discuss how to find a solution to a crisis that has pitted judges appointed under the former PiS government against those chosen by the current ruling coalition.

The prime minister today renewed that offer, inviting Nawrocki and his family to visit Tusk’s home in the build-up to Christmas. “We must be able to discuss things together, without bitterness, without hatred,” said the prime minister.

Note: This article has been updated to include the official estimate of attendance at the march.

]]> Poland and US sign statement of intent on strengthening defence industry cooperation https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/11/poland-and-us-sign-statement-of-intent-on-strengthening-defence-industry-cooperation/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 11:20:52 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106650

Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, have signed a statement of intent on strengthening cooperation between their defence industries.

“Today, we are taking the next steps in our alliance,” declared Hegseth, while Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the move signalled that Poland is now “not only a model ally…but has become a strategic partner of the United States”.

The Polish defence minister added that he would also push for equipment jointly manufactured by Poland and the US to be eligible for EU defence funding. “Poland is the US ambassador in the EU,” he declared.

Wicepremier W. @KosiniakKamysz z #Waszyngton: to chyba moja najważniejsza i przełomowa wizyta w USA. To moment, w którym mogę powiedzieć, że Polska jest nie tylko modelowym sojusznikiem, ale stała się strategicznym partnerem USA. pic.twitter.com/75xdgzIaG0

— Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) November 10, 2026

Kosiniak-Kamysz was welcomed by Hegseth in Washington to discuss a range of issues relating to security cooperation. A major item on the agenda was Poland’s desire for a new permanent US military base on its territory.

After the meeting, Kosiniak-Kamysz told reporters that there was a “green light from the Pentagon” for the base, with the final decision now resting with the White House. He said that was expected to be made in early December.

Hegseth, meanwhile, praised Poland for embracing the “NATO 3.0” concept, under which the US wants Europe to take on more responsibility for its own defence.

“Poland is building one of the most formidable armies in Europe, ready to secure and defend its territory,” said the Secretary of War, who noted that Warsaw is “leading by example” with its high levels of defence spending.

 

Hegseth also welcomed the fact that Poland is investing significantly in US equipment, including Abrams tanks, F-35 fighter jets, Apache helicopters and Patriot air-defence systems.

“You are building a fully modernised, interoperable force, and our two nations are…giving military cooperation industrial depth as well,” said the secretary of war.

Hegseth also reaffirmed Washington’s desire for a peace deal in Ukraine and “encouraged Kosiniak-Kamysz to continue Poland’s steadfast support of Ukraine”, said Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell.

American defense technology is driving innovation and creating new opportunities for transatlantic industrial cooperation.@USAmbNATO Matthew Whitaker, Assistant Secretary of Commerce David Fogel @CommerceGov and @USAmbPoland Tom Rose met with Deputy Minister of Defence… pic.twitter.com/5etw1L3X5A

— US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) November 10, 2026

Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the statement of intent he had signed with Hegseth was aimed at ensuring more US equipment was manufactured and maintained in Poland itself, including technology transfers.

He also said that he wants to secure European funds for jointly produced US equipment. The EU’s SAFE programme of defence loans, for example, largely excludes US manufacturers.

“We want American equipment manufactured by Polish-American companies to benefit from European funding. I will present such a position next Tuesday at the meeting of EU defence ministers,” said Kosiniak-Kamysz. “Poland is the US ambassador to the EU.”

The meeting between the two defence secretaries also coincided with the Transatlantic Defence Industry Access Forum, which brought together 70 Polish and 80 American firms, with the aim of strengthening ties between the two countries’ defence industries.

W ostatnich dniach dobra decyzja o utworzeniu w Polsce centrum serwisowego rakiet Patriot, a dziś podpisaliśmy kolejne porozumienie z USA, które przyspieszy współpracę naszych przemysłów zbrojeniowych.

Chcemy, by więcej uzbrojenia powstawało i było naprawiane w Polsce. To nowe… pic.twitter.com/j24E2xON66

— Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 10, 2026

Last month, the United States chose Poland as the location for a planned facility for servicing and maintaining Patriot missiles – the first to be located outside the US itself.

In July, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles. In May, an agreement was signed to establish a centre in Poland for servicing the engines of Abrams tanks.

That same month, President Donald Trump announced that his country would station an additional 5,000 troops in Poland, prompting Warsaw to formally request the establishment of a new US military base, which President Karol Nawrocki has suggested should be called “Fort Trump”.

]]> Two Ukrainians charged with spying and sabotage for Russia in Poland https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/10/two-ukrainians-charged-with-spying-and-sabotage-for-russia-in-poland/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 12:56:58 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106617

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Poland has detained and charged two Ukrainian citizens accused of carrying out espionage and acts of sabotage on behalf of Russia.

The men, aged 24 and 25, were allegedly paid to conduct reconnaissance of critical infrastructure and military facilities across Poland. They are also accused of setting fire to several vehicles with the aim of stoking anti-Ukrainian sentiment.

Funkcjonariusze Agencji Bezpieczeństwa Wewnętrznego zatrzymali w Mińsku Mazowieckim dwóch obywateli Ukrainy w wieku 24 i 25 lat podejrzanych o szpiegostwo i prowadzenie działań dywersyjnych na zlecenie rosyjskich służb specjalnych.
▶️ Mężczyźni rozpoznawali i robili zdjęcia… pic.twitter.com/G3i8hEsBHT

— Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 10, 2026

The suspects were detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) on 3 November in Mińsk Mazowiecki, a town just outside Warsaw, the capital. ABW officers also searched their residences and other locations connected to the investigation, seizing data storage devices and narcotics.

According to investigators, the suspects were tasked with setting vehicles on fire after changing their licence plates to ones used by Ukrainian military vehicles. This was “aimed at fueling anti-Ukrainian sentiment”, says the National Prosecutor’s Office.

Prosecutors have charged the men under Poland’s espionage law with working against Poland on behalf of a foreign intelligence service – a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of five years – and sabotage on behalf of foreign intelligence, which is punishable by 10 years to life.

At the prosecutor’s request, a court ordered both suspects to be placed in pretrial detention for three months.

 

In recent years, Poland has seen a huge rise in cases of espionage and sabotage carried out on behalf of Russia.

The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined.

Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe.

Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026

Last month, a Polish man was jailed for five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of an airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland.

Shortly afterwards, the trial began of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders.

In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage.

Poland’s justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, says that investigators have so far found “very strong traces of right-wing extremism” in the activity of Michał Oksiński, the man who carried out Saturday’s mass terrorist shooting in Kraków that left six people dead.
