By Aleks Szczerbiak

Poland’s escalating Constitutional Tribunal (TK) dispute is no longer simply a legal argument about contested appointments but a struggle over who defines constitutional legitimacy.

As the liberal-centrist government and right-wing opposition and president advance rival rule-of-law claims, the conflict risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent.

The roots of the crisis

Poland’s 15-member TK is a powerful body that rules on the constitutionality of the country’s laws. The roots of the current dispute trace back to late 2015 and began immediately prior to the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party taking office following its October parliamentary election victory.

In its final weeks in power, the outgoing government, led by the liberal-centrist Civic Platform (PO, now Civic Coalition: KO), fast-tracked the appointment of five tribunal members who were replacing those whose terms were set to expire in November and December.

Upon winning an outright parliamentary majority, the incoming PiS-led government refused to recognise these appointments, elected a slate of five new tribunal members, and party-backed President Andrzej Duda swore them in.

Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025

The tribunal (still largely composed of pre-2015 judges) ruled that three of the outgoing parliament’s appointments were lawful, so only two of the new ones could stand. PiS refused to accept this, creating the so-called “understudy” judges (dublerzy) controversy.

As further vacancies arose, the new parliament gradually installed its nominees, culminating in the appointment at the end of 2016 of one of them, Julia Przyłębska, as tribunal president. Przyłębska’s leadership was contested on procedural grounds, as was that of her 2024 successor Bogdan Święczkowski, a former senior prosecutor closely aligned with the 2015-23 PiS administration.

All of this led to the then-opposition parties and much of the Polish legal and the EU political establishments denouncing the tribunal as legally compromised and politically captured.

Total non-cooperation

Following the autumn 2023 parliamentary election, a new coalition government headed up by KO leader Donald Tusk embraced a policy of total non-cooperation with the tribunal, refusing to publish its rulings.

The battle for control took a new turn when, after initially not filling any tribunal vacancies, from March 2026 onwards the new parliament elected successive waves of new members, reaching eight by September.

However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki (who succeeded Duda in August 2025) refused to swear in five of these nominees, including former minister and close Tusk ally Maciej Berek. In response, the government took the unprecedented step of swearing in the contested nominees directly in parliament, a move that both Nawrocki and Święczkowski rejected as illegal.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

The conflict escalated sharply at the end of last month, when, backed by the government and tribunal members elected by the current parliamentary majority, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the five contested nominees but having the longest judicial tenure, asserted her seniority to order a one-month suspension of Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański in their official duties and assumed temporary control.

Justice minister Waldemar Żurek submitted requests to lift Święczkowski and Sochański’s immunity as the newly appointed members, and the new nominees entered the tribunal building under State Protection Service (UOP) escort.

This triggered protests by right-wing opposition supporters at the building’s gates, prompting a heavy police presence and tense stand-off. The severity of this was underscored when Nawrocki cut short an official visit to Senegal mid-flight, returned to Warsaw and entered the tribunal building in the early hours, condemning what he described as a violation of the constitutional order.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court.

The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

Korwin-Piotrowska then convened a tribunal general assembly which critics argued lacked the legally required two-thirds quorum because only eight of its 15 nominal members (the newly elected ones, including the five who had not taken the presidential oath) attended.

Her supporters maintained that the quorum was met because the suspension of Święczkowski and Sochański, and exclusion of the last remaining “understudy” judge, reduced the pool of eligible members to 12.

The government’s “transitional justice” logic

For the Tusk government and its legal defenders, these exceptional executive and parliamentary countermeasures were framed through the logic of “transitional justice”: as painful and extraordinary but necessary to restore the rule of law after PiS had violated the constitution and European standards, systematically packing the tribunal with political loyalists.

Justifying its non-recognition of tribunal rulings, the government argued that the presence of three defectively elected “understudy” members and their successors, together with Przyłębska’s and Święczkowski’s procedurally flawed presidential appointments, fundamentally “contaminated” the entire body, thereby invalidating its rulings.

In its efforts to restore democracy, the government may sometimes take actions that are “not fully compliant with the law”, admits @donaldtusk.

But he says this is because of the legal chaos deliberately created by the former PiS government https://t.co/AWlM6hRLie

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 11, 2024

To provide what it argued was authoritative external confirmation of this defect, the government relied heavily on landmark European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) and EU Court of Justice (CJEU) rulings which determined that, thus constituted, the tribunal could no longer be considered a legitimate body established by legal standards.

From this perspective, refusing to recognise the tribunal’s allegedly unlawful rulings was framed as the only available mechanism to neutralise a partisan weapon that PiS had left behind to block the government’s legislative agenda.

Alternative parliamentary swearing-in procedures were justified on the grounds that the president’s role in receiving oaths was purely ceremonial, not a constitutionally mandated requirement.

 

Despite his recent political role, Berek’s appointment was defended on the basis that he played more of a technocratic-expert role within the government, and was highly qualified to undertake the extraordinary transitional measures required to repair a damaged institution.

Defenders of the tribunal leadership’s suspension and occupation of its headquarters argued that by blocking the new nominees from taking up their roles, Święczkowski had paralysed the institution and decisive measures were necessary to restore its proper functioning.

A “coup d’état”?

PiS and Nawrocki, on the other hand, maintained that the Tusk government’s actions amounted to an authoritarian attempt to operate completely outside of constitutional powers, treating legality as an option when it conflicted with its political agenda.

They insisted that all of its 2015 appointments were in full accordance with the law, correcting an improper attempt by the outgoing PO-dominated parliament to entrench its influence after electoral defeat, and that the tribunal’s ruling on the legality of these three “understudy” judges went beyond its jurisdiction.

Successive tribunal general assemblies, they argued, validly and legally selected Przyłębska and then Święczkowski as presidents, and the Tusk government had no constitutional right to pick and choose which tribunal rulings it would recognise. They said that, by delaying the election of some new members when vacancies arose, the government violated existing procedures.

The constitution, they said, explicitly required these new nominees to take their oaths directly “before the president” and that by conducting improper parliamentary swearing-in ceremonies they had effectively renounced their offices.

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”

But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026

The candidacy of Berek, a recently active politician with doubtful professional qualifications, they said represented its own form of institutional capture and selective legality.

The suspension of the tribunal leadership and occupation of its headquarters amounted to an unlawful power grab or “coup d’état” that completely disregarded established constitutional procedures.

PiS rejected the “contamination” thesis and argued vigorously that Poland had never transferred jurisdiction over the organisation of the national judiciary to EU institutions and European courts, who had no authority to evaluate the legality of tribunal appointments.

They accused the EU political establishment of double standards, weaponising “rule-of-law” arguments to help a politically aligned government while ignoring the Tusk administration’s own executive overreach.

PiS also argued that by delegitimising a tribunal which had in the past ruled that the Polish Constitution superseded EU law, the Tusk government was paving the way for controversial social and economic policies to be pushed through without any domestic judicial oversight.

Tusk’s liberal critics

On the other hand, more ideologically supportive liberal critics of the Tusk government’s approach acknowledged the original 2015 irregularities but warned that selective non-recognition of an entire institution, combined with attempts to install a new tribunal without presidential participation, risked creating the same dual legitimacy problem that they accused PiS of having started.

They stressed that lasting repair required broad political consensus and careful adherence to formal procedures so that future majorities did not simply invert the non-recognition tactic. They noted the tension with earlier condemnations of PiS for elevating politically aligned figures or recently active politicians.

While sympathetic to the goal of reforming what they believed was a deeply compromised tribunal, these critics argued that, by employing legally questionable shortcuts and executive force, the Tusk government risked setting dangerous precedents and deepening the very disorder that it was claiming to correct.

Interestingly, the government’s broader “transitional justice” justificatory logic – that ordinary procedures would not adequately address a systemic capture and the priority had to be functional restoration rather than abstract purity – mirrored the arguments PiS itself advanced for its own judicial reforms after 2015.

The right-wing party argued that the post-1989 judiciary remained dominated by a post-communist elite that required deep structural overhaul rather than incremental change.

A high-risk escalation

The latest escalation is likely to entrench and intensify the profound systemic polarisation that characterises the Polish political scene, for a long-time embodied in the KO-PiS duopoly, with the conflict framed in existential terms of either “restoring the rule of law” or “defending the constitutional order”.

This fierce dispute lies at the heart of the Tusk government’s broader political “reckoning” (rozliczenie) agenda involving visibly removing PiS’s influence from key institutions.

For the ruling coalition, this was a central 2023 election campaign message, and being seen to deliver on it is an absolute political necessity to satisfy and mobilise its electoral base. A confrontational approach thus serves to consolidate the government’s support among these core voters, who have grown increasingly impatient and want to see decisive action.

However, the government’s strategy is fraught with political risk. High-stakes tactics risk uniting its right-wing opponents and alienating moderate voters increasingly exhausted by endless, hyper-partisan institutional confrontation, legal brinkmanship and the optics of police deployments around a key state body.

They provide the president and right-wing opposition with a powerful counternarrative of constitutional vandalism ahead of the next parliamentary election.

Escalation is also straining relations within the ruling coalition, especially among more conservative or legalistic coalition partners who believe that a more fundamental constitutional “reset” based on a cross-party settlement is required to break the impasse in the longer term.

The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has proposed a “constitutional reset” to resolve the crisis around the country’s top court.

It would involve removing all current judges and choosing new ones in a more consensual process https://t.co/xDwpRUVHxG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 6, 2026

Internationally, although the EU political establishment remains supportive of the Tusk government’s actions, they invite uneasy scrutiny of the stability of Poland’s legal system and have drawn explicit criticism from the US embassy.

The reliance on a “transitional justice” framing that echoes PiS’s earlier justifications for systemic change, combined with the appointment to the tribunal of a recent minister despite prior criticisms of politicised nominations, also undercuts government claims of consistent principle and provides the right with a powerful narrative of hypocrisy.

Legal dualism

Ultimately, this bitter dispute has paved the way for a protracted and deeply destabilising “legal dualism” that could plague the Polish state for years to come, with a tribunal simultaneously legitimate and illegitimate depending on who holds power.

By treating the tribunal as an illegitimate entity when its nominees did not control it, the current government has established a precedent.

Even if it now appears to have secured a clear majority for its own nominees, a future right-wing government and sympathetic president will have every incentive to use the exact same playbook: treating the reconstituted tribunal as a captured instrument of the liberal establishment, and regarding it as no more legitimate than the Tusk government did the PiS-era one.

Consequently, the tribunal’s authority, and legal certainty in Poland more generally, have been further eroded, leaving the country without a widely accepted arbiter to resolve constitutional disputes. There are no immediate prospects for a durable resolution of this conflict.

Thousands of soldiers from 11 countries began military exercises in Poland today. They are the first organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing, with the aim of preparing for a role in supporting Ukraine following a potential future peace deal with Russia.

The manoeuvres, which are being jointly led by France and the UK, are taking place in Nowa Dęba, around 100 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, and will last until 22 November.

The development has been condemned by Russia, which says it shows that Western countries are ignoring Moscow’s “legitimate security concerns” and “fueling the spiral of escalation”.​

The plans were first announced in July by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk following a summit of the Coalition of the Willing in Paris. The exercises, taking place on land, in the air, and at sea, are being conducted by the Multinational Force Ukraine (MNF-U), which serves as the military component of the coalition.

“This exercise will show that the Multinational Force-Ukraine is a real, capable, readily deployable force that represents a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine’s long-term stability and security,” said Tom Bateman, the British lieutenant-general commanding MNF-U.

The British Ministry of Defence says that the exercise, which has been named “Koalicja” (meaning “Coalition” in Polish), “will test Allies’ readiness to support Ukraine and rebuild their Armed Forces once the conflict ends”.

Poland’s defence ministry says the exercises will “demonstrate how quickly participating nations can mobilise and establish forces capable of supporting Ukraine after the end of the war”.

However, although Poland is hosting the manoeuvres, the defence ministry reiterated the country’s position that “it would not send its own soldiers to Ukrainian territory” as part of any postwar settlement. Poland has made clear it intends instead to help provide logistical support.

In the wake of Saturday’s deadly terrorist shooting in Kraków, a deputy defence minister has called for debate on limiting the number and types of weapons people can own. Meanwhile, a deputy interior minister says the tragedy provides an “incentive” to revisit proposals to better register certain guns.

Poland has among the lowest levels of gun ownership in Europe, though the number of firearms licences being issued has risen in recent years and some politicians have called for expanded access to guns. Saturday’s attack was carried out by a man who legally owned firearms.

On Saturday, 24-year-old Michał Oksiński drove through the historic city centre of Kraków, which was packed with tourists and locals, firing at random from his car.

He killed six people and injured over a dozen more. Later in the day, the bodies of the perpetrator’s parents and sister were found in his home, where they had been shot dead.

Oksiński’s rampage was brought to an end in a shootout with two police officers, which left all three with serious injuries. On Monday morning, the police announced that Oksiński had died in hospital. One of the police officers remains in what is described as “serious but stable” condition.

Speaking to Polsat News on Sunday, deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said that the tragedy “is the best illustration that it makes no sense to talk about expanding access to firearms”.

She added that “it’s already relatively easy” to obtain a gun licence, which can be granted to anyone aged 21 or over who has passed the relevant tests and declared that the firearm is for sporting purposes. Both Oksiński and his father had such licences and legally owned 11 firearms.

“I would like to start a discussion about whether access to such a large number of weapons should actually be so easy,” said Sobkowiak-Czarnecka. “This is also a question of whether someone who uses weapons for sporting purposes should have so many different types of weapons stored at home.”

Such weapons use traditional black powder rather than modern smokeless powder and include firearms manufactured before 1885 and their modern replicas.

Although gun ownership in Poland is relatively low, it has been rising steadily in recent years, particularly since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with the total number of registered firearms owned by Poles surpassing 1 million, up from around 380,000 in 2014.

Under Polish law, civilians can apply for licences for sporting, hunting, collecting and personal protection purposes. To obtain one, applicants must undergo medical examinations, pass a test, and join a relevant association, such as the Polish Sports Shooting Association, the Polish Hunting Association, or a collectors’ group.

Licences for sports and collection purposes are the most popular types of permits, together making up 76% of last year’s permits. But the number of licences issued for “personal protection” has grown from just 81 in 2021 to 7,254 last year.

A record 50,709 gun licences were issued in Poland last year and the total number of registered firearms has now surpassed 1 million.

Gun ownership in Poland has risen particularly rapidly since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 https://t.co/axt2YS044Z

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 11, 2026

Access to firearms widened in 2023 under the former government, when parliament passed a law removing “unnecessary administrative and legal barriers.” That allowed members of uniformed services to apply for personal protection permits, a change lawmakers said was intended to “strengthen Poland’s defence potential”.

However, some politicians, especially on the right, have pushed for ownership rules to be further loosened. In September, speaking at the opening of a shooting range, President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, called for “public discussion about responsible access to weapons”.

“Even in the European Union, Poland remains at the bottom of the list in terms of access to firearms,” he said, quoted by Polsat. “Only about 1% of Polish citizens have access to weapons and are skilled at using them. Fortunately, I’m in that 1%.”

They were attending a “retreat and gala” hosted by CPAC, which also organises a major annual conservative political conference and has close ties to Trump. The cheapest tickets to attend the gala cost $2,500, ranging up to $7,500 for VIP access.

Blask Online’s photos show Ziobro eating dinner at the event and speaking to former British Prime Minister Liz Truss. Trump himself addressed the guests, saying that he “wants to congratulate everybody here”.

From 2015 to 2023, Ziobro served as justice minister in a PiS-led government, overseeing judicial reforms that are widely seen as having undermined the rule of law.

After a new, more liberal ruling coalition led by the current prime minister, Donald Tusk, took power in December 2023, it launched a number of investigations into the actions of senior PiS officials.

That led, last year, to prosecutors announcing that they want to charge Ziobro with 26 crimes, including leading a criminal group and approving the unlawful purchase of Pegasus spyware, which was used to surveil some of PiS’s political opponents.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Thu, 12 Nov 2026 09:33:49 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Introducing the Christopher Ward C1 Bel Canto Lucia https://www.cityam.com/introducing-the-christopher-ward-c1-bel-canto-lucia/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 10:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2475705

Beauty is in the eye of the beholder. It can leave you speechless. It might stop you in your tracks and make you do a double take. The Christopher Ward C1 Bel Canto Lucia does all of the above. This is a beautiful watch; no doubt about that, not beautiful as in a writer’s throwaway [...]]]>

Beauty is in the eye of the beholder. It can leave you speechless. It might stop you in your tracks and make you do a double take. The Christopher Ward C1 Bel Canto Lucia does all of the above.

This is a beautiful watch; no doubt about that, not beautiful as in a writer’s throwaway line, but beautiful as in stunning, the kind you need to see firsthand to confirm you were not dreaming.

The kind of watch you need to see on your wrist, the kind that makes you imagine how the light plays with the dial at different times of the day.

The kind of watch that finds you daydreaming, staring at its face and saying to yourself, “Man, that’s one fine watch”. The kind of watch you can lose your heart to, too.

Named after the lead character of Donizetti’s opera Lucia di Lammermoor, the Bel Canto Lucia takes inspiration from one of its most famous scenes, in which Lucia sings about a bird that only she can see.

The Bel Canto Lucia’s predecessor

The Bel Canto Lucia’s predecessor, the Christopher Ward C1 Bel Canto, showcased a chiming skeletonised complication. In a fortuitous twist of fate, admirers of that watch could not help but notice how the exposed hourly striking mechanism of the FS01 chiming module resembled a bird on the dial. And so a myth was born.

“People started pointing out very early on that FS01’s chiming works looked a bit like a bird. The slightly embarrassing truth is that this wasn’t necessarily intentional – the desired symmetry of the mechanism led us there,” says Christopher Ward Product Director Jörg Bader.

Bader goes on to explain, “With Lucia, Mr Jones Watches has taken that happy accident and turned it into something very real. The challenge for us was ensuring that the artwork could become part of the mechanism itself, with the beak and tail retaining genuine mechanical functions.”

The C1 Bel Canto Lucia follows in the footsteps of 2025’s C1 Celestial Moonphase, the first watch collaboration between Christopher Ward and Mr Jones Watches. Its 300-piece run sold out in less than 48 hours and was subsequently nominated at the Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève (GPHG).

In light of its well-deserved success, talk turned to how the two companies could collaborate again, this time with a more technically ambitious brief: to integrate Mr Jones Watches’ artwork directly with the mechanical architecture of the watch.

On the Lucia, that resemblance to a bird is no longer left to one’s imagination. The mythical beast has become an integral working part of the watch, a songbird at its centre. The position of its beak tells you whether the chime is engaged: when the pusher at four o’clock is pressed, a delightful rotating bug mounted on the column wheel prompts the bird to open or close its beak.

Its tail has a rather more exciting job: for it is the hammer that delivers the hourly D note. It really is serendipity in motion.

“The Bel Canto watch was a dream to design for,” says illustrator and watch designer Andy Wilx. “I wanted to create a world you could peer into, and with so much space between the mechanism and crystal, I was able to create a design with real depth.”

Assembly

The bird isn’t simply painted onto the dial. It is assembled from six separate stamped brass pieces that travel to Mr Jones Watches, where each one undergoes a painstaking production process.

Here, the bird’s framing elements are gold-plated. The scene’s striking colours are applied using a traditional dial pad-printing process. Each and every colour requires its own printing plate and needs repeated applications to give Andy Wilx’s stunning design the grand treatment it deserves.

Layers and layers of ink are printed on an artwork measured in millimetres, as each of the 19 individual colours is laid down with the precision and dexterity that would make a heart surgeon proud.

Once finished, the individual components are precisely aligned and laminated together using custom jigs developed specifically for the project.

The completed assemblies are then returned to Christopher Ward’s Atelier in Biel for final assembly onto the movement. This makes Mr Jones Watches an integral part of the manufacturing process of each C1 Bel Canto Lucia, rather than merely the source of its artwork. The result is striking.

If the watch sounds anywhere near as good as it looks, it’s truly a masterpiece, but nothing less than you would expect from Christopher Ward, one of the most magnificent disruptive innovators in modern watchmaking, who has now turned disruption into an art form.

The C1 Bel Canto Lucia joins the Christopher Ward Atelier Collection as an open-series model and is available from £3,995. To listen to the FS01 module yourself and view its superb artwork in person, book an appointment at the Christopher Ward showroom, or secure yours directly at christopherward.com.

Shares in Burberry soared after the British fashion house returned to profit off the back of renewed demand for its iconic trench coat. 

The FTSE 100 group took a £19m pre-tax profit in the six months to the end of September, recovering from its £48m loss at the same time last year, as its revenue grew six per cent to £1.1bn. Shares in the group gained seven per cent in early trading to 1,166p.

Burberry chief executive Joshua Schulman has sought to return the fashion house to the mid-market by cutting prices and boosting the visibility of its well-known trench coats since he was appointed in 2024. 

The fashion house told shareholders on Thursday that sales of its outerwear products grew by double digits in the period, driven by demand for its rainwear. 

Burberry said it saw “particularly good growth” in sales of its tropical gabardine, a variation of its iconic trench coat which sells for about £1,795. 

The group also saw strong demand for its cropped trench coats over the summer. This new design, which is available at a lower price point than the full-length trench, has been one of the ways Schulman has sought to make Burberry more affordable. 

His arrival at Burberry followed the fashion house’s short-lived foray into ultra-high fashion, which prompted a period of falling sales as its aggressive price hikes alienated scores of consumers. 

Cotswolds fever boosts Burberry

Schulman has also sought to arrest the luxury group’s declines in China – a crucial market for Burberry which had declined in the period before his appointment. Sales in Greater China were up nine per cent in the first quarter of Burberry’s financial year, though this growth has slowed to five per cent in recent months. 

In recent months, Burberry has capitalised on the growing popularity of the Cotswolds with wealthy Americans, introducing a new handbag design named after the sought-after English region, some of which sell for more than £2,000. 

The fashion house said sales of its leather goods have accelerated in recent months, driven by growing demand for its Cotswolds and vintage-check handbags.

Schulman said: “Two years ago, we launched Burberry Forward. Today, our brand and our business are stronger. Five consecutive quarters of growth and improved quality of sales demonstrate that our strategy is working.

“Having laid the foundations for growth, I am more confident than ever that we will realise the full potential of this extraordinary British luxury brand.”

]]> 2476989Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong Neets tsar Milburn says benefits overhaul will lead to savings ‘in a decade’ https://www.cityam.com/neets-tsar-milburn-says-benefits-overhaul-will-lead-to-savings-in-a-decade/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 08:48:43 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2476983

The youth unemployment tsar Alan Milburn has called for people under 25 to be blocked from sickness and disability benefits although potential savings on the welfare bill could take a decade before they are realised.  Ahead of his report’s publication, Milburn said young people should no longer claim benefits as he argued that the welfare [...]]]>

The youth unemployment tsar Alan Milburn has called for people under 25 to be blocked from sickness and disability benefits although potential savings on the welfare bill could take a decade before they are realised. 

Ahead of his report’s publication, Milburn said young people should no longer claim benefits as he argued that the welfare system should focus on employment investment, mental health support and helping people build a “good life”. 

The review into youth joblessness is expected to lead Andy Burnham into introducing major welfare reforms aimed at helping people get into work and reducing a bill of about £146bn when child benefits and pensioner spending are excluded. 

The Prime Minister has previously said he did not want to “see anybody in their 20s on benefits in this country”. 

Milburn’s welfare proposals

Under Milburn’s plan, young people would instead be moved onto a “youth allowance”, paid at the same rate as Universal Credit, under his proposals. Those who receive disability payments would get additional cover relating to their condition and it would not be means tested. 

A new benefit would also be introduced for those who are not capable of working. 

He said nearly 1m people aged between 18 and 24 who are not in education, employment or training, who are referred to as ‘Neets’, would be presented with a “menu of options” to enter the national workforce. 

Investments in the near term would be “significant” under the former health secretary’s proposals, which could put additional pressures on public finances. 

“Obviously this costs money,” he told The Times in an interview. 

“And frankly it’s a better use of money — both from the point of view of the young person and the taxpayer — to spend that money getting them into work rather than … keeping them on benefits. This is the sort of fatuous thing about this debate. You’ve got to invest upfront in order to get savings out of the back end. ‘Cost-free’ is fatuous. So we’ve got to be candid about that. It will need significant investment.

Even with further spending on employment support and health, Milburn warned that proposed reforms in next week’s report could lead to a pinch on young people’s budgets. 

‘This will not be easy’

“I’m not saying that any of this will be easy, or that it will be pain-free, because it won’t,” he said.

“Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system. But actually, for young people, there’s a different debate that we’ve got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances.

“I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that’s the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around.”

Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, will respond to the Milburn review after it is published in full next week. 

A government plan on welfare, however, may not come until February at the earliest, according to Chancellor John Healey. The government is also set to consider recommendations in the Sir Stephen Timms review on disability payments, which is not expected to consider the financial implications of welfare spending. 

An interim report of the Milburn review suggested that the ‘Neets’ crisis cost the UK economy up to £125bn a year from lost output and higher welfare spending. 

Initial findings by the Neets tsar also found that for every £1 the Department of Works and Pensions spent on employment support for young people, around £25 was spent on benefits for young people.

The boss of WH Smith has blamed the retailer’s woes on its “forced growth” under previous management, as a sharp fall in profit undermined the group’s hunt for a turnaround.

The London-listed travel retailer posted a £76m pre-tax profit in the year to the end August, 28 per cent lower than last year. After multiple profit warnings earlier this year the group had cut its target to £75m, having initially hoped for as much as £115m.

Leo Quinn, the turnaround specialist who took charge of WH Smith in April, said he has begun “a fundamental reset” of the group as it battles soft consumer confidence and travel disruption caused by the Iran war.

The group’s executive chairman, who previously led comebacks at Balfour Beatty and Qinetiq, said it had suffered from “forced growth” which resulted in “increased costs, too many loss-making stores, acquisitions not integrated effectively and high organisational complexity”. 

Quinn said WH Smith’s UK division, which includes stores at airports, train stations and hospitals, was forced to cut marketing spend and discount more products in response to “weaker consumer sentiment”. 

The group’s shops at hospitals performed the best, with revenue growing nine per cent, compared to three per cent at its train station stores. Takings across WH Smith’s UK arm grew four per cent to £870m.

WH Smith told shareholders that its suppliers have adopted a more “cautious” approach in response to the “macroeconomic and geopolitical backdrop” caused by the conflict int he Middle East. 

The firm, which is newly reliant on its airport stores after selling its high street estate last year, had been forced to issue multiple profit warnings throughout the year, as the Iran war causes travel disruption and pushes up the cost of flying, resulting in lower consumer spend at airports.

WH Smith saw its airport business grow by just one per cent on a like-for-like basis, with the group blaming “the macro environment and reduction in passengers”. 

Flat US sales weigh on growth

The retailer’s revenue grew by nine per cent to £437m at its beleaguered North American arm, which was beset by an accounting scandal after it emerged that its profit in the region had been flattered for years. 

But the group blamed lower passenger volumes in North America for its stalling growth at the start of the new financial year, as like-for-like growth was flat in the 10 weeks to 7 November.

Conroy Gaynor, a senior consumer analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said: “Our view remains that the company is in the midst of a difficult turnaround, with likely headwinds to earnings at least in the near term.”

Quinn said his “complex” turnaround plan will “transform WHSmith over the medium-term into a Group capable of generating attractive returns, with significant annual free cash flow.”

Metro Bank has put itself up for sale as the high street lender explores potential takeover offers following a turnaround of the business in recent years.

The London-listed bank announced on Thursday that it had launched a formal sale process as part of a wider strategic review aimed at accelerating growth and maximising returns for shareholders.

Metro Bank has appointed Morgan Stanley to oversee the process and invited potential buyers to submit expressions of interest for the entire company.

However, the lender stressed that it was not currently in talks with any potential bidders and had received no takeover approaches.

The move comes after Metro Bank completed a major restructuring that helped it return to profitability following years of financial difficulties.

The move comes after Metro Bank reported its most profitable half-year on record in August, with pre-tax profits jumping 41 per cent to £60.7m in the six months to June.

The bank, which operates 78 branches across the UK, has undergone a major restructuring since 2023, shifting away from mainstream lending towards higher-margin commercial and specialist loans.

Its core target lending book, covering corporate, small business and specialist mortgages, grew 43 per cent year-on-year to £6.2bn in the first half.

“The significant progress made by Metro Bank means it is now well positioned to consider a broader range of strategic opportunities for its next phase of growth,” the lender said.

The board added that exploring potential takeover interest alongside its existing strategy would “maximise the value creation opportunities available to shareholders”.

Metro Bank eyes next phase of growth

The potential sale follows a string of changes at the challenger bank, including the departure of chairman Robert Sharpe at the end of October after six years in the role.

Senior independent director Catherine Brown was appointed interim chair, subject to regulatory approval, while the bank began searching for a permanent replacement.

Metro Bank has also continued expanding its physical footprint despite a wider industry retreat from high street branches, signing leases for new sites in Newcastle, Leeds and Nottingham earlier this year.

The lender reaffirmed its profitability targets last week, forecasting a return on tangible equity of more than 13 per cent in the final quarter of 2026, rising to more than 15 per cent next year and 18 per cent in 2028.

The bank said its directors unanimously supported exploring a potential sale alongside continuing its existing growth strategy.

Under the formal sale process, interested buyers will be able to hold confidential discussions without being publicly identified or facing the usual 28-day deadline to make a firm offer.

Nvidia’s board is reportedly meeting to decide whether to oust chief executive Jensen Huang after revelations of a second extramarital affair, this time with an executive at the chip giant, sent its shares plunging.

The company’s directors are weighing the future of its billionaire founder following reports that Huang had a relationship with a female Nvidia executive who reported directly to him, according to the New York Times.

The new allegations come just days after Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife amid an investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman suspected by US intelligence officials of working for China.

Nvidia shares fell around eight per cent in after-hours trading on Wednesday after the Wall Street Journal reported that the company was preparing to remove its chief executive.

The latest decline brings Nvidia’s losses to roughly $600bn (£452bn) in market value this week, as investors weigh the prospect of losing the man who has led the world’s dominant AI chipmaker for more than three decades.

Nvidia’s board is reportedly meeting to discuss whether to dismiss Huang, although no decision has been announced.

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a memo to employees on Sunday, taking “full responsibility” but offering no details about the relationship.

The controversy initially centred on Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom US intelligence officials suspect of facilitating shipments of Nvidia chips to Chinese companies.

National security risks under review

The suspected affairs add growing scrutiny in Washington over Nvidia’s dealings with China and whether Huang’s personal relationships posed national security risks.

Democratic senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have called on the Trump administration to preserve documents relating to Nvidia’s chip exports and Huang’s alleged relationship with a Chinese intelligence operative.

In a letter to senior officials, the senators warned that the incident raised “significant concerns” about the government’s ability to enforce export controls and protect national security.

Republican lawmakers have also threatened to subpoena Huang unless he agrees to brief Congress on Nvidia’s security procedures and his interactions with Alice Huang.

John Moolenaar, chairman of the House committee on China, said lawmakers wanted to establish whether Beijing had accessed sensitive information or influenced US policy.

President Donald Trump, who has maintained close ties with Huang, confirmed earlier this week that the FBI was investigating the allegations but defended the Nvidia boss.

“I know the FBI is looking into it,” Trump told reporters, adding that Huang had assured him he was unaware of the woman’s alleged intelligence connections. “I really believe him”, he said.

The crisis has raised questions over Nvidia’s succession plans, with Huang owning around 3.6 per cent of the company and no publicly identified replacement.

The 63-year-old co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has overseen its transformation into one of the world’s most valuable companies, supplying the chips underpinning the global AI boom.

His potential departure could unsettle an industry already grappling with concerns over the vast sums being poured into artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Elon Musk weighed in on Wednesday, saying it would “be an honour” to hire Huang after an investor suggested the Tesla boss should recruit him.

Musk also backed calls for Nvidia’s board to await the outcome of its investigation before making a decision.

The UK economy grew by 0.7 per cent between July and September, official data has shown, as spending held up in the face of a spike in energy prices caused by the Iran war. 

The Office for National Statistics said GDP expanded far above previous expectations in the third quarter of 2026, with economists revising up forecasts in recent weeks. It is the fastest quarterly growth figure in more than two years and brings the UK back to averages seen around 10 years ago.

Over the month of September, the UK economy grew 0.2 per cent, compared to projections of zero growth. 

New figures showed that the services sector grew 0.9 per cent over a three-month period, while production expanded by 0.1 per cent and construction fell 0.7 per cent.

“The economy grew robustly in the third quarter almost entirely due to strong and widespread growth in the services sector,” said Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS.

“Within services, computer programming again increased strongly, as it has all year, registering its fastest growth in the last three years. We continue to see evidence that AI-linked businesses helped to boost this sector.”

Underlying figures showed that business investment was up by 0.4 per cent in the last quarter and about three per cent higher than the same time last year. Most services sub-sectors grew while household consumption was also higher in the third quarter than in the second three-month period of the year.

In an unusual intervention, Prime Minister Andy Burnham directly commented on the latest figures.

““This is welcome news,” Burnham said. “Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future.

“Our job now is to keep focused on what matters to people: bringing down bills, creating good jobs, helping high streets thrive, and backing businesses to grow.”

In a separate statement, Chancellor John Healey said the UK economy was showing “stand-out resilience” and growing at the “fastest rate in almost ten years, outside the pandemic” after data showed that GDP was about 1.9 per cent higher than the same quarter a year ago.

UK economy benefits from AI investment

The latest set of data reflects relative strength in the UK economy this year despite a series of warnings that higher international oil and gas prices would dampen activity. 

The Bank of England indicated last week that about a fifth of growth was driven by AI-related investment. Independent figures by Bloomberg Economics suggested about a fifth of the expansion in GDP was due to AI. 

In the first three months of the year, growth came in at 0.6 per cent, followed by 0.5 per cent in the second quarter. 

The data suggests that growth this year is expected to far outpace expectations set by economists last year, who had predicted an improvement in GDP of as low as below one per cent. Lord Jim O’Neill, the former Goldman Sachs executive and close ally to Andy Burnham, recently said annualised growth was closer to two per cent and suggested markets could be off the mark in assumptions about the UK economy. 

Forecasters looking ahead to next year have pencilled in dramatically different figures for growth in 2027. 

The Office for Budget Responsibility suggested that the effects of the energy price spike from conflicts in the Middle East would kick in next year, dragging growth down to one per cent. 

On Wednesday, the National Institute of Economic and Social Research said growth next year would edge up by 1.1 per cent. 

]]> 2476868Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar Hyrox wants to be in the Olympics but at what cost for triathlon? https://www.cityam.com/hyrox-wants-to-be-in-the-olympics-but-at-what-cost-for-triathlon/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 07:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2476604

I hold my hand up: two weeks ago I referenced the Hyrox founder’s ambition for his hybrid training venture to become part of the Olympics. Ended my sentence with a dot dot dot. I hold my hand up: two weeks ago I referenced the Hyrox founder’s ambition for his hybrid training venture to become part of the Olympics. Ended my sentence with a dot dot dot. Might as well have rolled my eyes. 

Within days, however, World Triathlon had announced that it was admitting Hyrox into its federation, and hence into the wider Olympic family, if not (at this stage) into the Olympics itself.

Details are sketchy for now. What’s in it for World Triathlon? Has money changed hands, or will it, in either direction? Has World Triathlon committed to lobby for Hyrox events to be part of Brisbane 2032 or a subsequent Games? 

If so, would WT be prepared for any of its existing Olympic disciplines to make way, or does it believe it could persuade the IOC to oust events from another sport with lesser appeal to younger generations?

Some elite triathletes have voiced concerns. Not every Hyrox adherent is overjoyed either – is courting the sporting establishment on brand?

“For us this is terrible… We’re still in for LA but who knows after that? It’s definitely concerning for the future of our sport and for the younger generations coming up,” triathlete Max Stapley told The Telegraph.

“We are paving the way for an entire generation of hybrid racers to chase their own Olympic dream,” says Moritz Furste, Hyrox co-founder.

Triathlon participation numbers around the world are well below their peaks. The sport – once a young challenger itself, only entering the Olympics at Sydney 2000 – caters increasingly to an older demographic.

While smaller in athlete numbers, Hyrox continues to grow apace with around 1.5m participants in the past year. It will need to demonstrate durable growth if it is to convince the International Olympic Committee of its merits. Only time will tell whether hitching its power sled to World Triathlon is the optimal way to do that given the obvious inter-discipline conflicts that will doubtless fester.

The IOC will decide on the Brisbane 2032 sport programme in April next year. A tight timeline for the newly married couple to work to.

Seems there’s no simple noun for a Hyrox athlete equivalent to triathlete. A void that needs filling, surely? Hyroxian, hyroxlete, hylete, hyroxter, hoxster, hyrocker?

Additionality

Every day is a school day. Mine on Monday was in the House of Lords where we launched a report on the social impact of wheelchair rugby and I learned about additionality. 

Primarily an economic term, in sporting studies it can refer to net social effects and is especially relevant to a sport such as ours which caters to individuals with often severe impairments and who might not otherwise be able to take part in any fitness activity at all.

The comparison we were asked to make by the report’s author was between his own sporting choices – if he wasn’t playing tennis he might well be on a golf course or a bike or out running – and those available to wheelchair users. 

Tennis could disappear and the net effect on the nation’s health, after a period of adjustment, might be slim. Remove wheelchair rugby and hundreds of players might fail to find an alternative physical and social outlet.

Dawn of the Planet of the Apes

I ran around Battersea Park just after dawn yesterday morning and now know what it must be like to be a tailrunner. 

I was passed by scores of runners in both directions, most under half my age I guess, the males among them – who were firmly in the gender minority – trailing the odour of the previous evening’s Lynx in their wake.

Evidence of the continued Gen Z running boom, or instead were these healthy specimens all getting in their pre-work Hyrox training? The park’s 400m track appeared very busy, in spite of the early hour, as I peered through its chainlink surround. 8am reps? Probably confirms my hybrid suspicion.

Strangers on a train

Overheard on the train en route to Selhurst on Sunday.

Stranger #1: “I need to get out at the next stop. Where are you going?”

Stranger #2: “Going up to Twickenham. Just got a call to say my friend had a spare ticket for the rugby.”

Stranger #1: “That’s nice. I’ve never been. Is it league or union?”

Stranger #2: (Thinks for a long while) “Union, I guess.”

Hope #2 enjoyed the match. A man from Mars would surely be just as baffled at the existence of two rugby codes.

Glad all over (still)

Bottom of the league but you wouldn’t know it from the mood on my return journey from Selhurst. We Crystal Palace fans have often been here before. 

At the time of writing, manager Pierre Sage, much liked in the stands, is still in his job. My hope is that the club winning its first meaningful trophies in the past two seasons hasn’t hexed our recovery prospects. 

Never dull, always fun, wouldn’t have it any other way. Can they say that in the Stretford End?

    Walking through the door of Number 10 Downing Street was one of the proudest moments of my life. I grew up in a council house, raised by a single mother, and never imagined I would one day be helping the Prime Minister tackle the cost-of-living crisis.

    It was an extraordinary privilege. Number 10 has an almost magical power to bring people together. Make a call from Downing Street and people answer. They listen. They want to help.

    But I also discovered something deeply frustrating. If you were designing an organisation to run a modern country, you wouldn’t design Number 10. The fragmentation, endless meetings and lack of accountability would be unthinkable in a successful business.

    I remember sitting through a roundtable involving 28 important people, including senior politicians and business leaders. Everyone had their say, then everyone went away. But I asked one simple question: what will be different tomorrow because we met today? The answer was virtually nothing.

    That experience crystallised a wider concern about how Britain is run. We have become a country that talks endlessly about growth while systematically discouraging the people who deliver it.

    And nowhere is that contradiction more damaging than in our attitude towards wealth creators.

    I helped build Just Eat from a struggling start-up into a business worth £5.5bn. We nearly went bust twice. We worked extraordinary hours, we took enormous risks and we created jobs in Britain – even when it might have made more financial sense to create them elsewhere.

    I am proud of that. Why shouldn’t I be? Yet increasingly, successful entrepreneurs are made to feel that their achievements are something to apologise for. When did ambition become a crime?

    The highest-earning one per cent of taxpayers contribute roughly a third of income tax revenues. The top 10 per cent contribute around 60 per cent. These are the people helping to fund our hospitals, schools, pensions and public services. So why are we sending them the message that we don’t particularly want them here?

    I work with investors and entrepreneurs who are genuinely relocating to Milan, Portugal and elsewhere. These aren’t theoretical threats, people really are leaving. And when they go, we don’t just lose their taxes. We lose their investment, their businesses, the salaries they pay and the opportunities they might have created for the next generation.

    Worse still, think what this tells a young person growing up in a council house today.

    My mother had a simple philosophy: no excuses. Work hard, take responsibility and get on with it. That mindset helped change my life. I want every young person in Britain to share that same self-belief, but instead, we’re creating a culture in which success is resented rather than celebrated, while too many young people are left without work, training or purpose.

    This is where Andy Burnham has a choice to make. And I’m worried he’s already wasting his best opportunity to make it.

    He arrived in Downing Street with enormous political capital, a fresh mandate for change and the ability to take difficult decisions. Yet his first Budget was painfully timid.     Worse, he looks to be continuing the very policies and attitudes that have driven Britain’s wealth creators away. A new leader cannot simply inherit a failed strategy and carry on implementing it. No successful business would tolerate that.

    Burnham is a good communicator. He should use that skill to win the argument for growth, not hide behind the manifesto of his predecessor. He should tell Britain that wealth creation is something to celebrate, not punish.

    Because Britain doesn’t need fewer successful people. It desperately needs more.

    Yet more Tube strikes in the run up to Christmas risk making calls for a driverless Tube network irresistible, argues James Ford

    As Father Christmas is making his list of who has been naughty and who has been nice this year, one suspects that, somewhere near the top of the naughty list, will be the name Eddie Dempsey. He is the General Secretary of the RMT union and the man who, this week, has announced his union’s intention of holding no fewer than eight days of strike action between November and February. Three of those strike days will be in the run-up to Christmas, including the last Saturday before Christmas Day (which is such a huge day for retailers that it is dubbed “Super Saturday” or even “Panic Saturday” in the industry). What a Grinch.

    But Eddie Dempsey is not just risking getting a piece of coal in his stocking this year. Rising RMT militancy is making it harder and harder to justify the continued existence of Tube drivers at all. The more that the unions choose to inconvenience Londoners, the more sympathetic Londoners become to the idea of a driverless underground. We’ve had more than 160 days of strike action under Mayor of London Sadiq Khan, which is more than three times as many strikes as happened under both of his predecessors at City Hall combined. (And that is despite Khan ironically pledging that there would be zero strikes if he was elected Mayor).

    It may surprise readers to learn that much of the Tube is already partially automated. On only three Tube lines – the Piccadilly, the Bakerloo and the Waterloo & City – do the drivers actually drive the trains. On the eight remaining lines, the so-called ‘drivers’ just open and close the doors in stations and the business of accelerating and braking is computerised. This is called Automatic Train Operation (ATO) and is known in industry jargon as “Grade of Automation 2” (GoA2). The Docklands Light Railway is GoA3 because, while it is driverless, a member staff – the Passenger Service Agent – is still onboard. The ultimate goal though must be fully unmanned operation (GoA4). That would make the London Underground strike-proof. GoA4 train systems are prevalent in other major cities: the Riyadh metro, the Dubai Metro, Singapore’s Mass Rapid Transit, the Vancouver SkyTrain, and the Copenhagen Metro. There are no fewer than 33 GoA4 metro systems in the USA and even Paris has three fully automated Metro lines. In the UK, however, fully automated transport systems are currently just used for airport transit, like Heathrow’s Terminal 5 Transit and the AirRail link in Birmingham. 

    Traditionally, the biggest barrier to making the Tube fully driverless has been cost rather than public anxiety over driverless technology. Afterall, the DLR has been automated since 1987 and it was used for 90.8m passenger journeys in the last financial year. Sadly, new signalling, platform edge doors, more modern trains and other upgrades are required before the Underground can truly embrace going driverless. Transport for London (TfL) estimated that it would cost £20bn to fully automate the three oldest Tube lines (the Central line, the Bakerloo Line and the Piccadilly Line), with the Central Line alone costing an eye-watering £10bn to upgrade. 

    But changes in the Budget last month might have made the high cost of adoption less of an issue than it was before. Plans to fully devolve business rates to local Mayors by the end of the decade could mean that an extra £9bn a year of funding is on the table. Given the GLA’s spending in 2026/27 was £22.9bn, that is a potential huge boost, even before we factor in the £10bn of extra borrowing that the Budget unlocked too. Whilst TfL had hoped to invest much of this windfall in extending Tube lines and improved stations, perhaps a significant proportion could instead be redirected to finally make the Tube driverless.

    Currently, the RMT is able to hold the capital to ransom with impunity. Anti-strike legislation is the cheapest solution to London’s Tube union problem but the current Labour government overturned the law that would have given Londoners some respite from the union bullies. Going driverless would give London a Tube network that is more resilient and reliable, breaking the RMT’s stranglehold on the capital’s economy. And Eddie Dempsey might just get back on Santa’s nice list.

    Pound shop PM bargains on rescue

    A pound shop prime minister? That might seem a harshly premature verdict on Andy Burnham, but framed in the context of Britain’s latest high street crisis, it may just be appropriate.

    It’s far from irrational that Burnham has intervened in the crisis at Poundland, and not only because his Makerfield constituency is home to the discount chain’s largest distribution centre.

    “This is a deeply worrying time for Poundland staff and their families,” the PM said a couple of weeks ago. “We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn’t been accepted, then the business secretary and I want to know why that is the case.”

    Events since those words, however, imply an alarming degree of government impotence. Until this week, Gordon Brothers, Poundland’s majority-owner, had shown complete contempt for its management, employees – and by extension Burnham’s administration – by freezing access to the chain’s finances.

    A claim to be focused solely on an outcome which preserved jobs has rung hollow as Gordon Brothers failed to progress solvent bids with little more than disdain. One, from Martin Property Group, the Londonderry-based business which owns the rump of National Car Parks, could have been concluded weeks ago. That it was not appears to have been dictated by its disinclination to line Gordon Brothers’ pockets.

    Importantly, Pepco Group, Poundland’s Warsaw-listed former owner, still retains both a minority equity stake in the chain and a 25 per cent interest in a £30m loan, the bulk of which is owed to Gordon Brothers. Pepco has offered to defer its right to repayment on condition of a solvent deal, suggesting that it at least understands the gravity of the situation.

    Belatedly, Gordon Brothers released limited funds to Poundland this week to provide a stay of execution – but this looked cynically timed to coincide with yesterday’s business and trade select committee grilling.

    This has all the hallmarks of the most pointless major retail collapse for decades and the most politically contentious since BHS in 2016. Vulture capitalism is an overused label, but the evidence here leads to the conclusion that it’s a wholly appropriate one.

    Ditching annual say on pay would be a mistake

    Should the say on pay have had its day? The government’s latest consultation on overhauling Britain’s corporate governance regime is a microcosm of its schizophrenic approach to regulating British business: pile needless red tape on companies while removing some of the guardrails which actually serve a useful purpose.

    Shareholders’ right to an annual advisory vote on executive pay – derided by some as no more useful than the proverbial chocolate teapot – is under threat, part of a potential corporate governance bonfire being assembled by ministers to demonstrate their commitment to supporting economic growth.

    They’ve chosen the wrong target, though. Companies including AstraZeneca, Glencore and, as I revealed this week on Sky News, LSEG, owner of the London Stock Exchange, are all consulting major shareholders on significant increases to executive pay packages amid growing anxiety in the City that more blue-chip companies will flee to the US.

    A spokesperson for the Investment Association told me: “The advisory vote on remuneration is an important mechanism for shareholder accountability and helps maintain alignment between pay, company performance and shareholder interests. While we support efforts to modernise corporate reporting, its removal could have unintended consequences, including greater opposition to directors’ re-election and a more stringent approach to remuneration policy votes, ultimately reducing flexibility for companies. We will make the case for retaining this vote.”

    They are right to do so. The annual say on pay provides a useful guardrail for boards, making them accountable to their shareholders. Stop the votes, and it’ll make it harder for companies to argue that trying to keep pace with overseas competitors is a valid endeavour – and that would be to the long-term detriment of corporate Britain.

    A troupe of finance bros are swapping the trading floor for the dance floor. Anna Moloney reports

    When I meet Adam Lyons, dressed casually in a hoodie and jacket at the bottom of the Royal Exchange steps, he immediately apologises: “I’m not in my look!”. And indeed, waiting for Lyons at one of the busiest junctions in the Square Mile, I had had to stop myself several times from approaching other men for whom Lyons’ “look” – black trousers, white shirt and, most important of all, a gilet – is simply their everyday attire.

    For Lyons though, his gilet has become the trademark not so much of the trading floor as the dancefloor, having garnered over 500m views online for videos in which he and his merry troup of finance bros groove in sync to modern pop hits around the City
    of London.

    Their first video to take off was a flashmob in 2024 in Liverpool Street Station to the then-viral “I’m looking for a man in finance”, and Lyons has been grooving in his gilet ever since. Lyons tells me he now dances in the Square Mile at least three times a week, often for content collaborations for big-name companies, with Charles Tyrwhitt, Farmer J and Reiss just some of the brands that have approached him to dance with their products.

    I first came across the troupe myself while walking across the City for a meeting, only to be stopped in my tracks by the striking sight of an apparent finance bro hairwhipping on all fours to Miley Cyrus’s Bass Persuades upon the base of the Duke of Wellington statue. Lyons giggles when I tell him that was my introduction to his work.

    ‘I feel at home in the City’

    Lyons, who grew up in Liverpool with a deep love for girl bands, said he always wanted to move to London and felt a particular draw to the financial district, which he coveted less for its career prospects than its drama.

    “I’ve always thought this looked like a stage,” he says, gesturing to probably the City’s most iconic backdrop – the Royal Exchange forecourt where the neoclassical columns of the old stock exchange are flanked by new shiny blue skyscrapers – which serves as the main set piece for almost all Lyons’ videos. “There’s so much that looks like it could be for a concert set. I always try to use the statue and the stairs,” he says, adding that when he first saw a particular group of columns by the Bank of England he immediately thought of a specific Ariana Grande awards performance which he could recreate there.

    It is captivating to talk to Lyons and see the City through his eyes, not as a place to get off the Tube and shuffle to one’s office (as many view it), but as a hub of awe and creativity. “This is my favourite place in all of London,” Lyons says without a hint of insincerity. When first coming to the City, it was naturally an intimidating place, but Lyons says he now feels at home in the financial district. “People really accept me here and I feel like I have a community around here.” The staff in Starbucks all know him and he says he regularly gets recognised from his videos.

    Are finance bros now sexy?

    Throughout our conversation, Lyons is at pains to emphasise his bit is not designed to mock financial workers, or their sense of style. “I just want to be clear that I’m not here to take the mick,” he says, adding how much he genuinely loves his gilet. “I actually find it really hot and sexy. It’s a smart look. It’s a classy look. Doesn’t everyone fancy a finance bro?”

    Cloud 9 | National Theatre | ★★★☆☆

    First staged in 1979, Caryl Churchill’s Cloud 9 was once considered a sensational, salacious and provocative piece of theatre. Nearly 50 years later, Dominic Cooke’s National Theatre revival doesn’t pack the same punch.

    It’s a play of two halves, both in structure and setting. The first act takes place in Victorian colonial Africa, opening with the cast singing an imperial anthem before patriarch Clive (Sam Troughton) introduces his family. Wife Betty, children Edward and Victoria, governess Ellen, mother-in-law Maud and servant Joshua all exist under his strict patriarchal rule. Sexual repression, gender conformity and racism are the order of the day. There isn’t much in the way of conventional plot; instead, we see the family romp through a series of interactions with one another. It’s satirical and slapstick, but disturbing, too.

    The second act leaps forward to “present day” 1979, though the characters only age 25 years. Watching it in 2026, we are almost as far removed from the era of the second act as Churchill was from the first when she wrote the play. Naturally, then, many of its observations have lost their cutting edge.

    What has aged badly in Caryl Churchill’s Cloud 9

    Some aspects of the production have inevitably evolved; Joshua, Clive’s black servant, was originally written for a white actor but is now portrayed (brilliantly) by Eloka Ivo. But other elements feel awkwardly outdated. The play’s treatment of topics such as incest or corporal punishment of children reflects a 1970s permissive outlook that’s at odds with the rest of the progressive piece.

    Whatever its inconsistencies, the production is carried by a wildly versatile cast and the whole thing serves as something of an actor’s showcase. It’s a technical feat by Rebecca Humphries in particular, who plays both the repressed governess Ellen and the liberated family friend Mrs Saunders in act one, only to return unrecognisable as the edgy Lin in act two. Likewise, having spent the first act playing nine-year-old Edward, Ellen Robertson stands out in the second act as the older, divorced Betty, delivering a particularly stirring monologue about marriage and liberation. While ironic and amusing, the cross-casting does read as a little on the nose when the patriarchal colonialist Clive later plays demanding toddler Cathy (an entertaining and crowd-pleasing switch-up by Troughton).

    Miriam Buether’s stage design is a visual spectacle. So much so that any stragglers still in their seats during the interval are gently ushered out to make way for an elaborate set change. What Buether does with the second half is interesting and unnerving, not least because the audience spends it under the exposing glare of the house lights.

    Cloud 9 at the National Theatre: A fascinating historical piece more than a play for today

    At 88 years old, Churchill is still going strong as one of our greatest living playwrights. Her oeuvre has consistently demonstrated a great skill for responding to our time, but this revival doesn’t make the case for Cloud 9 as a play for today. That doesn’t lessen its importance – much of the intersectional gender, sexual and racial dynamics are still relevant – but overall makes it feel more like a fascinating historical piece than a work of theatre offering a fresh perspective.

    In contrast, Churchill’s latest satire Triumph debuted at the Almeida earlier this year, about the blonde press secretary of an unnamed American president. Triumph had a lot more to say in its 15-minute run time than this revival does in nearly three hours. If you missed it, fear not: more of Churchill’s new short plays are to be staged at the Almeida next year as part of Dominic Cooke’s first season as artistic director (he’s evidently a fan). I expect those will be as powerful now as Cloud 9 was then.

    It was also noted in Healey’s committee hearing that the health department, which is normally protected from proposed cuts, would have to identify cuts to fund extra defence investment, though he said the department would “manage” to protect “vital services”.

    He said officials across Whitehall were currently “preparing and contributing” to ideas for the 10-year plan. 

    Following the plan’s publication, Healey indicated that all focus across the government would turn to the Spending Review, which reportedly has been pushed back until the end of 2027. Burnham refused to say on Wednesday when the review would take place.

    Shortly after taking to Downing Street, Burnham and Healey wrote to Cabinet colleagues to demand they identify savings.  

    “The Prime Minister and I – and you will have seen this from day one – have worked in lockstep on fiscal discipline and on fiscal restraint across government,” Healey said. 

    “We will be running next year’s Spending Review as one that will be jointly-run between Number 10 and Number 11.”

    Healey also argued that the Labour government’s proposal to reform the triple lock pension, which could take about 14 years before delivering savings worth about £15bn, would be crucial to the next Spending Review as it would feature “bigger and longer-term decisions”.
